subtopic: POWER TO PROHIBIT SOUND SIGNALS AT CROSSINGS IN OR NEAR CITIES AND TOWNS

speechtext: Mr. A. R. ADAMSON (York West) moved for leave to introduce bill No. 8, to amend the Railway Act.

subtopic: POWER TO PROHIBIT SOUND SIGNALS AT CROSSINGS IN OR NEAR CITIES AND TOWNS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: POWER TO PROHIBIT SOUND SIGNALS AT CROSSINGS IN OR NEAR CITIES AND TOWNS
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to amend sections 308 and 419 of the Railway act.
The amendment .grants power to certain municipalities contiguous to or near large cities to pass by-laws prohibiting the sounding of the statutory crossing whistle at specified grade crossings within the confines of such municipality.
The reason for this amendment is that many townships or villages situated contiguous to major metropolitan areas have now become so built up that they constitute a physical part of the neighbouring city or town.
Railways passing through these built-up areas and whistling at the crossings constitute a nuisance and are a real menace to the health and welfare of the residents of such districts.

Argentina-Canadian Nationals

The amendment is simple in form as it merely adds the words "township or village situated contiguous to or near such city or town" to subsection 2 of section 308 of the Railway act, and the same words to subsection 3, section 419, of the same act, the latter being the penalty clause and' contingent on section 308.
Subsection 2 of section 308 will now read:
"(2) Where a municipal by-law of a city or town, or of a 'township or village situated contiguous to or near such city or town, prohibits such sounding of the whistle or such ringing of the bell in respect of any such crossing or crossings within the limits of such city or town, or township or village, such by-law shall, if approved by 'an order of 'the board, to the extent of such prohibition relieve the company and its employees from the duty imposed by this section."
This does not constitute a blanket order permitting all townships or villages to pass prohibitory by-laws, nor does it embrace all grade crossings in the designated municipality, as each crossing must under the terms of the act be approved by the board of transport commissioners, who must be satisfied as to the safety measures taken at each crossing where the whistle warning is to be dispensed with.
I would mention the case of St. Hilaire Village v. Canadian National Railway, where it is shown that relief can only be obtained by an amendment to the act.
Motion agreed to and bill read; the first time. ARGENTINA

speechtext:
I should like to make a statement to the house which will serve in part as a further answer to some of the questions which have been asked on the orders of the day this afternoon. I hope the house will not object to the length of the statement, but it is important, and for that reason I have tried to anticipate and cover some of the questions I thought might be in the minds of hon. members.
In answer to a question by the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) on Friday of last week, I said that I hoped I could find it possible at an early date to talk over questions of mutual concern with members of the United Kingdom government. I have been waiting until the address in reply to the speech from the throne has been agreed to, to inform hon. members of what I have in mind, and of my present intentions. As my plans have been made on the expectation that, at a first session, the debate on the address would not likely continue longer than three weeks from the opening of parliament, which period expires to-day, I feel I should not delay longer in making to the house the statement I had hoped to make at the conclusion of the debate.
External Affairs

The world is still in a very troubled state. The war is over and the victory won, but the responsibilities that rest on governments are not perceptibly lighter. We have our own task of reconstruction in Canada, but to carry it out as wisely and as well as we should wish it is essential that consultation be had from time to time with members of other governments, facing similar problems, often under more difficult circumstances.
These last months have seen many changes in Europe, brought new persons into responsible office and faced them with new problems. We in Canada are directly concerned with the solutions which they are seeking to these problems. Experience has taught us that the problems of other countries very quickly become our problems as well.
The process of peace-making is obviously going to be difficult and protracted. The task is not one of restoring the world as we knew it before the war. That world has gone. The collective task is to get the new world moving along paths that will lead to peace, happiness and the general welfare. This means finding ways in which the peoples of the world can work together in confidence and cooperation.
In the shaping of the new world order, a good start must be made in the right direction during these next critical months. Decisions that will have to be taken during the coming months may shape and determine the kind of world we are going to live in. I am not thinking primarily of the particular questions that the council of foreign ministers has been considering at its recent meetings. Questions of boundaries, of colonial administration or regional disarmament are important, but, in the last analysis, many of them are of less consequence, even to the countries whose interests they affect most immediately, than are questions of attitudes and objectives. These are, as I see it, the big questions, the worrying questions. They are hard to formulate and harder still to answer. What kind of world do we really wish to live in? What sort of effort are we ready to make to realize it? What do we and what do people in other countries mean when we agree that peace and prosperity are indivisible in this one world? How can we help each other to make our world a free world in which we can give substance to the idea for which free men died?
We should find working answers to these questions and find them without delay; for, on the answers which we in Canada and other countries give to these questions, national policies must be based. It is the answers to these general questions which will determine
[Mr. Mackenzie King.l
what we should do about defence; how we can most wisely and effectively maintain high levels of employment and promote a fairer distribution of a larger national income; and how far, as a country, we can go in attempting to assist the economic recovery of our allies and the restoration of the world trade on which our wealth and welfare have depended.
Hon. members will be aware that during the meetings in London of the council of foreign ministers the question of participation by nations of the British commonwealth, apart from the United Kingdom, has arisen on a number of occasions.
The Canadian interest in the meetings of the council of foreign ministers lay not so much in the detailed discussions of particular issues, as, for example, the demarcation of frontiers, as in an overriding concern for the peaceful settlement of outstanding differences, and for consolidating the general organization for the maintenance of international security.
It is important that Canada should not merely be consulted, but that there should be clear recognition of Canada's right to effective participation in the great decisions where questions affecting the general ordering of the future peace of the world are under consideration. During the war, for military reasons, it was necessary to acquiesce in the operation of war-time arrangements under which responsibility for major decisions on the direction of the allied war effort was concentrated in a very few hands. The continued use of methods such as were improvised to meet the urgent strain and hazards of war, whereby private settlements are arrived at between the great powers on issues of general interest, might well become a source of difficulty and even of danger. Every possible precaution should, therefore, be taken to see that in this particular the war-time pattern is not perpetuated in the framing of the peace settlement and in the united nations organization.
It is with these thoughts in mind that I have decided I should, as soon as possible, make an informal and, if necessary, an extended visit to the United Kingdom and western Europe.
Of conditions in Europe generally, I should like to obtain first-hand information from my own observation and inquiries. If I am to have the knowledge of many of the problems which are now upon the horizon, and to be able to speak regarding them with the authority I should like to possess, I feel that I should see for myself something of the changed world in which Canada must make her way and take her part.
The operations of UNRRA, the general conditions of food, clothing and shelter in

External Affairs
the war-devastated countries of Europe, are all of concern to Canada as a principal supplying agency under various international arrangements. Apart from the practical working of these arrangements, there is a still greater humanitarian interest which wrill continue to have a strong claim upon our capacity to help in the relieving of suffering and distress.
I would hope, while in Europe, to have an opportunity to visit areas occupied by Canadian soldiers, and the scenes of battles with which, through the heroic exploits of our fighting men, the name of Canada will ever be associated. I think it is important also that I should visit Canada's embassies and legations, some of which have been established since the beginning of the war, and all of which, in consequence of the war and postwar problems, have had to operate under new and difficult circumstances.
It was on August 24 that Mr. Attlee, in a personal message to myself, stated that he would greatly welcome it if I and other prime ministers of the commonwealth felt we would be able to come to London for purposes of consultation and personal discussion at the opening of the council of foreign ministers. At the same time, Mr. Attlee stated he regretted to have to raise such proposals at such short notice and that the United Kingdom government recognized the great difficulties which this might involve for me and for the other prime ministers. When Mr. Attlee's telegram was received, the present parliament had been summoned to meet on September 6, and it was, as Mr. Attlee himself recognized, not possible for me, because of the opening of the first session of a new parliament to visit London at that time. Until I had met parliament and confidence in the government had been expressed by the House of Commons, it would not have done for me to be absent from Canada. That confidence has been expressed in the votes thus far recorded in the divisions which have taken place on the amendments moved by the Progressive Conservative party, the C.C.F. party and the Social Credit party to the motion of thanks to His Excellency for His Excellency's speech addressed to both houses of parliament.
It is now, therefore, possible for me to take the house into my confidence with respect to the reasons which make it advisable that I should pay the extended visit I have referred to. Having assured Mr. Attlee that I would, at an early opportunity, be glad to talk over with him matters of mutual interest to our governments, I feel I should avail myself of the opportunity which now presents itself for this and the other purposes
I have mentioned, and which, if not availed of at this first session, may not be possible in the period between the close of the present session and the next session which will come in the new year. My plans have, accordingly, been made to leave for London early in the coming week.

On the orders of the day:
Mir. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River):	I
should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. In the light of the serious strike of southern Alberta miners, will the government give consideration to some change in the meat rationing regulations to permit of a more equitable distribution of available meat supplies-recognizing the principle of greater need on the part of those engaged in heavy work such as miners, lumbermen, etcetera?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DIFFERENTIAL RATIONING FOR MINERS, LUMBERMEN, ETC.
speechtext: A great deal of consideration has been given to the question whether differential rationing, as it is called, is practicable and the decision arrived at is that it is not. The request of the miners in Alberta, at least the group referred to in the question, is that they receive double rations. Naturally if they were to receive double rations, claims would arise from many other groups in various parts of 'Canada. The question, in so far as lumber camps are concerned, is answered by an arrangement that is made apart from change in the number of pounds per week of meat available. That is, in remote districts where alternative food supplies are not available in large measure, the rationing authorities make available extra quantities of meat, not by way of individual quota but by way of quotas such as a restaurant or some such establishment gets, and the situation is covered in that way. But the specific request here, to allow more pounds of meat per week to certain classes in the community, is deemed to be impracticable. At the same time I may say that the rationing authorities are giving much attention to the problem of how to relieve cases of particular hardship. They have not been able to find any solution to the problem as yet, but it is receiving attention at the present time.

May I ask the Minister of Justice a question. On Tuesday I sent him a copy of a telegram which had been sent me by the attorney general of Saskatchewan. Can he give us now the information requested in that telegram?
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of
Justice):	When the original question was
put the other day I attempted to answer it from memory, and probably I should not have done so because I find there were some errors in the information I gave the house at that time. Thus I referred to the Dominion Land Mortgage Association and I am informed that it is the Dominion Mortgage and Investments Association. I also stated that information had been given to the attorney general of Saskatchewan almost as soon as the petitions had been received. When I received, later on Tuesday, the telegram addressed to me by the attorney general of Saskatchewan I immediately referred it to the deputy minister of justice and he has supplied me with this information. The petition of the Dominion Mortgage and Investments Association was received early in July. Mr. Carson, of Toronto, acting as counsel for the petitioners, saw the deputy minister of justice just about that time, and there was some discussion as to whether he wanted to add any oral representations to those contained in the petition. What was determined then was that he did not feel that it was necessary that he do so, but if we wished for further elaboration of the representations in the petition he would be available. The petition was then referred to the law officer who deals, as a matter of course, with the examination of all the provincial legislation adopted each year, and who prepares memoranda to enable recommendations to be made to council as to whether or not the legislation should be allowed to have such operation as it can legally have. In considering this legislation an effort is made by the law officers, who have considerable experience in that matter, to study everything that is pertinent to the form and purport of the legislation, whether representations or petitions come in or not. The only additional value there can be in making representations is to focus attention upon something which, in spite of their experience, the law officers might not consider pertinent or consider that it was necessary for them to study and report upon.
It was only when the other petition for disallowance came in from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company specifically requesting a hearing that the matter was dealt with in any other than the routine way. That request was received at the department on September 16. The deputy minister wrote to counsel for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and to Mr. Carson, as counsel for the other party that had made the representation, on September 18, asking them to send copies of their representations to the attorney general of
House oj Commons

Saskatchewan, in view of the fact that it appeared they wished to be heard orally. As I say, those letters were written on September 18, and I understand that copies of the representations were supplied to the attorney general on September 20. Those letters suggested that they could be heard if they wished on October 11 and on October 15, as I stated before.
There is not going to be any trial of issues at that time. Council will of course be allowed to make such representations as they see fit to make, and those representations will be considered, together with the legislation itself, as an aid in the preparation of the recommendations that are made in every instance with respect to provincial statutes.

My point of privilege, Mr. Speaker, is that we cannot hear what the Prime Minister and ministers of the crown are saying. I might say to Your Honour that sometimes we cannot hear what you are saying. We can never hear what the leader of the opposition is saying. It seems that we cannot hear what anybody is saying. I doubt, Mr. Speaker, whether you can sometimes hear- you are straining your ear a little bit even now while I am speaking-what we are saying. The press gallery cannot hear; the spectators cannot bear; nobody can hear what anybody is saying.
May I now ask the Prime Minister a question? Since the British parliament leads the way-the Prime Minister is putting his hand to his ear now, which proves my point that the ministers cannot hear-would the Prime Minister give consideration soon, and before he goes away, if possible, to the matter of installing some system of amplifiers in this chamber?

The house resumed from Wednesday, September 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. W. Benidiclcson for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Ross (Souris), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Wright.

The Address-Mr. Townley-Smith
Mr. F. W. TOWNLEY-SMITH (North Battleford):	Mr. Speaker, when the house
adjourned yesterday I was discussing floor prices, parity prices, and a proper percentage of the nation's income so necessary to the western farmers. I am sure all hon. members realize there will be some difficulty in establishing those parity prices. However, it can be done. It will be a job for our mathematicians and our research men, but I am convinced they can do it.
The point I wish to make here is that it will be necessary to have those prices established before we can indicate what ninety per cent would amount to. Hon. members in this group do not like the ninety per cent stipulation. We do not see any particular advantage in pussyfooting around with a part of the parity price and we would ask for the establishment of the whole of it. In our subamendment we ask for the establishment of floor prices for all basic agricultural products on a parity with other services and products. The hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Tucker) yesterday said that his government was in favour of parity prices; hon. members will find that at page 472 of Hansard. He also said at page 484 of Hansard:	We
want one hundred per cent. The logical conclusion for one to arrive at would be that the hon. member for Rosthem and his fellow members will vote in favour of our subamendment. But of course, Mr. Speaker, I am only a new member.
There is a feeling prevalent in this country that the farmer to-day is well off and has lots of money in his pocket. That is true within certain limits. It is true, as a matter of fact, that the war, and the war only, has been responsible for the farmer's receiving better prices for his products; but the principal reason that he has money in his jeans to-day is that he has not been able to spend it upon the things which he really requires to buy. If he had been able to buy the machinery he requires and pay for needed repairs to his machinery and paint for his buildings and a host of other things, he would not have this money in his pocket. The farmer himself will receive a surprise, perhaps a shock, when the time comes that he is able to buy the things he requires to reequip his farmstead. As a matter of fact his wealth is superficial, not real. He has the money at the present moment but when he has bought some of these $1,700 tractors and' $3,000 combines his money will rapidly disappear. I would like hon. members especially those who have just a passing knowledge of agriculture, to bear that in mind when they hear talk about the western 
farmer rolling in wealth at the present time. He is a pretty good fellow. He has been very patriotic and loyal and he has given willingly of his sons and daughters and of his dollars to the war effort, and now in his old age he has gone into harness again, with his womenfolk helping him, to see that the production of food is not decreased because of the exodus of so much of his help.
And so, Mr. Speaker, I would say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), who made a statement on the price of western wheat the other day: Let us say to the people of devastated Europe and to the people of the low countries: Not only here is wheat but here are flour and foods of all kinds, both in bulk and otherwise; here are clothes; here are machines, boots and shoes, pots and pans, building materials of all kinds, and the prices of all of them are being held down to the level of September 19, 1945.
May I say this about world markets, to which we farmers will have to subscribe and to which we shall have to adjust ourselves. I believe that when the smoke of battle has finally blown away, every country will be compelled to produce that which it can most economically and most easily produce. Thus it may be that in certain parts of Canada which are at the present time extensively engaged in dairying, the harsh winters, the great distance from tidewater and high freight rates will not permit our farmers to compete with countries like New Zealand and Australia, with an outdoor climate that is moderate all the year round, and with their closeness to the sea. It is conceivable that some other country may find that they can produce and get their products on to the world markets more cheaply than we. That possibiliy must be faced, and we must be ready for it, even though the quality of our products is higher.
We have been accused by members in certain parts of this house of having communists as friends. They are no friends of ours, Mr. Speaker. In fact, many of them tried to prevent me from getting down here at all. However, these same communists were advocating a coalition with the Liberals, and so it would be just as logical to refer to them as friends of the Liberals.
Great changes are taking place all over the world, and there is a great change taking place in this country. The poet Tennyson saw that many years ago when he wrote:
Ring out a slowly dying cause,
And ancient forms of party strife;
Ring in the nobler modes of life,
With sweeter manners, purer laws.

The Address-Mr. Senn
Tennyson saw this thing coming. We in this group, sir, are anxious to help the government in all the legislation which they introduce in this difficult period, if they in turn will show that they are sincere by bringing down legislation that will be helpful to all classes. But there must be no indifference and no complacency. Serious situations will arise calling for careful handling, and it will tax the efforts of all hon. members of this house working together to smooth out these situations and make this great country of ours a good place for all classes to live in.

Mr. Speaker, it has been my custom always when addressing this august chamber to be as brief as possible, and I am going to follow that practice to-day. I had not intended to take part in this debate on the address at all, until the night before last when my colleague the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) introduced an amendment which he asked me to second.
When the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) made his statement in the house on September 19 in regard to setting a floor price for wheat, it was of course not debatable but I did ask him whether the provisions of the order in council applied to winter wheat grown in the eastern provinces, and I was glad indeed to hear his statement that it was not included. One dollar a bushel may have been a fair price at one time for winter wheat, but it is not so to-day. With higher costs of production, higher costs of labour, higher taxes, and other factors that enter into production, it is not profitable today to produce wheat in the province of Ontario at $1 a bushel. It is true of course that our eastern crop of wheat does not loom nearly as large as the western crop; we produce only some 25,000,000 bushels in the eastern provinces. On the other hand, the sale of that wheat forms an important part of the income of many farmers in eastern Canada. Moreover, wheat production works very well with their particular crop rotation. For these reasons I should like to see a fair price established for winter wheat in eastern Canada.
Although the minister's statement was of prime importance to the wheat growers of the west, I believe it was equally important to other branches of agriculture than that of growing wheat. I think we must accept this statement as an indication of government policy respecting the farmers' price structure. I regarded it as such as soon as that statement was made, and that is the reason I seconded the amendment of the hon. member for Souris. That my fears in this respect are
altogether too well grounded was amply demonstrated, I think, yesterday when the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) spoke on behalf of the government. He said that this was the first step in implementing the provisions of Bill 168, which was passed in 1944 and was called the Agricultural Prices Support Act. He read a certain clause in the act which he said provided for adequate and stable returns for agriculture. But I am afraid that this act is not going to work out as he expected, for it has some important defects.
Unfortunately I happened to be away on the week-end in 1944 when this bill was introduced, and did not have a chance to discuss it and to express my criticisms. But so far as I can understand, it has at least two important defects. The first defect is that the provisions of the bill are only temporary in character. The title: of the bill as it was brought down in the House of Commons is, "An Act for the Support of the Prices of Agricultural Products during the Transition from War to Peace." The question arises right away^-and I think the farmers of the country are particularly interested in this: What is this period of transition? How long is it going to last? Is it to be one year or two years or perhaps five years; and after that period of transition is over, what is going to happen next? The farmer, more than anybody else in the: country, needs permanence and stability. The great thing which has affected the prosperity of farmers in days gone by is that there have been many rapid and violent fluctuations in farm prices, and this bill is to be operative only after prices fall. The board provided in the bill will not step in until such time as it thinks prices have gone below the proper level. The farmer would like to know, I should like to know, and I think everybody in the house would like to know, to what level must prices fall before this bill becomes operative, before the board which has been set up will step in and try to do something -with this revolving fund of $200 million which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is so glad to mention from time to time.
Just in passing I might remark that the time has arrived in at least one branch of agriculture for putting this revolving fund into effect. There has been and there exists at the present time a grave congestion of cattle on our live stock markets, and particularly in our stock-yards. This congestion has caused prices to fall, in some cases to unprofitable levels. It should be the duty of this government and of the board which is set up under this act to provide in some way for
The Address-Mr. Senn

these heavy runs, if necessary to take a certain amount of the revolving fund and remove these cattle from the market.
I know the minister made the statement the other day that farmers should be careful to market their cattle and hogs in a more orderly manner. But it is not always possible to do so. When a hog gets to a certain weight it must be marketed, or the farmer loses by reason of a lower price; it passes into another grade and he is using his feed to very little advantage. The same is true very largely of cattle, perhaps for a different reason. When cattle are well finished they should go on the market; but there are times in the fall when the farmer has to raise money, and the only way he can do so is by sending his cattle to the market. He may also be in a position where he has to get rid of these cattle or they will be kept at a loss. In passing I would recommend to the minister and his board that provision should be made now to deal with the congestion of cattle which occurs in our stock-yards and on our markets from time to time, and which could very well be handled by this board and this revolving fund. This is not the first- time that this condition has occurred in the fall; as a matter of fact it happens every fall; and some permanent provision should be made by the government or by some suitable authority to see that this does not occur from time to time to the farmer's detriment by reason of its effect in lowering prices.
Farmers should know in sufficient time what prices they are going to receive for their products. They must make their plans a long time ahead. If a farmer is going to market a field of grain, that field must be ploughed, in eastern Canada at least, a year ahead, and I take it that the same is largely true in western Canada. If he is producing hogs or milk or beef cattle he has to make his plans even further ahead; and as I have already said, from time to time, after he has made hds plans on the assumption that a certain price then prevailing will continue, he finds that by the time his product is ready to market the price has fallen, fluctuations in price have taken place, and the result is he does not get the returns that he should receive for his cattle and other products.
May I also point out that if reasonable floor prices were established for all classes of goods which the farmer is likely to produce, he is a good enough judge to know whether he can produce those goods at those particular prices. If he cannot produce hogs profitably, perhaps he can turn to beef, or milk, or grain, or some other article for which he is sure he will reap a reasonable reward. But I am

afraid that if the price which has been set on wheat by the minister is any indication of the level of prices which are to be set for other classes of farm products, the farmer will be in greater difficulties than ever. On this phase of the matter I still think that bill 168, providing for fair prices in the manner in which the government has seen fit to present it, is unsatisfactory, and that it will not -establish parity prices or fair prices to the farmer if the wheat price that has been set is to be the measuring stick by which we must measure what the government will do in all other cases.
This act does not come in until the War Measures Act goes out, that is, six months after the war.

The Act does not apply to
wheat, but in any case, whether the bill can be of use at the present time, something should be done to see that prices do not fall unduly.
May I now refer to a certain clause in the speech from the throne relating to agricultural matters and primary industries.
The maintenance of long-term markets for our primary industries is receiving close attention. The continuing need for foodstuffs, both at home and abroad, will ensure, for some time to come, a heavy demand for the products of our farms and fisheries. .
That clause lays stress upon the value of the export market and upon the value of the home market; they are both important to the farmer. I would say however that, if anything, the home market is even more important than the foreign market particularly in eastern Canada. For a great many years, up to a short time ago, nearly ninety per cent of everything the farmer produced in Canada was consumed in Canada in one way or another. The exception to that rule was wheat, and the percentage in the case of western wheat was a good deal larger. However, during the war there were certain classes of farm products that were produced in greater quantities, and we were glad to be able to export them in greater quantities.
The minister brought down a correction of the figures he placed on Hansard the other day when he was speaking. I have taken those figures that were put on Hansard and have made a computation, and I find that for the past eight years, 1938-1945, we have exported about thirty-three per cent of our pork and about twelve per cent of our beef. If I am correctly informed, and I read the question which the leader of the C.C.F. party asked the minister, that included meat sent overseas to feed the troops while there. If those troops come back they will have to be fed here and it will mean that a smaller per-

The Address-Mr. Senn
centage of our total production will be sent overseas. In addition the minister tried to prove to us, and I believe he convinced us, that if we did not have greater grain production in the near future our production figures in cattle and hogs and other live stocks would go down and go down very rapidly.
Every one will agree, I think, that these years have been years of high production during the war. Taken altogether, production of grains in Canada and everything else on the farm has been much higher than it was prior to that time. We have had bumper crops, and those crops have helped us to maintain the supplies we so much needed. There is one thing I would suggest to the government in passing, and that is that we should if possible try to retain our British market for bacon. It is one of the best we have. If we receive a fair price for our production of bacon, it is one of the most profitable lines the farmer in Canada can follow.
AVhen the Minister of Agriculture was speaking the other day he took credit for establishing floors by means of contracts which he had negotiated with Great Britain, and he claimed, and I think rightly, that the prices set by those contracts set the floor price of farm products in Canada, at least of bacon and beef and perhaps cheese. I would point this out, however. Those contracts were negotiated in a seller's market. The desperate need which Britain had for foodstuffs enabled the government during the difficult times when those contracts were negotiated to get better prices than they might otherwise have obtained. That is one reason why I am afraid of the announcement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
What is the effect of that announcement, in reality, particularly as to certain markets we have? I think the effect of that announcement has been to serve notice on our customers abroad that the government of this country has embarked on a policy of deflation of farm prices. I do not think we can draw any other conclusion than that, and the result will be, I am afraid, that instead of being able to negotiate contracts in a seller's market in the future we shall have to bargain in a customer's market where the customers in different countries will be able to dictate the prices we can obtain for different classes of goods.
It is undoubtedly true, and no one will deny it, that low export prices means low domestic prices. I can recall in a good many instances in days gone by, and not so long ago either, that in certain classes of farm products we
had only a surplus of five or ten per cent, and the small price we had to take for the exportable surplus had a direct bearing on the domestic price. That is not as it should be.
The next thing I would point out is this. After all, primary production is the greatest factor in creating buying power in Canada. There are four broad branches of primary production in Canada: farming, mining, fishing and lumbering. Of these I do not think anyone will deny that agriculture is the most important. It is the most important from the point of view of financial returns, and it is most important from the point of view of population. From 28 to 30 per cent of the population of Canada are farmers, but in addition to that there is a large body of people who are engaged in collecting, transporting, processing and marketing our farm products. If you take all these together it is safe to say that they form the largest consuming group in Canada. As such if the farmers of Canada are prosperous and can buy, then other classes in the community will be prosperous, because the farmers will consume to the extent of their ability and income.
I suggest therefore that the first objective of any government should be at this time to fix parity prices. There has been some discussion in the house as to what the term "parity prices" means. I do not intend to give any scientific explanation of the matter. I think a simple sentence will outline what parity really is. It is a fair relationship between farm prices and the prices of goods and services which the farmer has to buy. That ig_ simple enough. Moreover, if the farmer is given a fair price he will produce. There is no doubt about that. He will produce to the limit of his ability. The thing he needs and the thing he should have is this. He should know that he will get a fair price, and that as time goes on, between the time he makes his plans and the time he gets his goods on the market, there is not going to be such a slump that he will be unable to carry on.
I think we all agree at the present time that farmers are enjoying a fair share of prosperity, or at least partial prosperity. The hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Townley-Smith) gave a reason or two for that. The first is that undoubtedly during the war, prices have gone up. Whether the government is going to take credit for that, or whether it is due to something over which nobody in this country has any particular control, I shall leave it to parliament itself to judge. But I do say that even with the prices that prevail, the farmer has not yet had a fair share of the national income. That is true because after price ceilings were set
The Address-Mr. Senn

up the government found it was impossible for the farmers to carry on in that way, and they introduced a system of subsidies on different kinds of farm products. I think that in the year 1944 those subsidies amounted to over a hundred million dollars.
That is just the direct subsidies.

Yes; there were others as well. Some were paid by the Department of Agriculture and some by the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation, and perhaps some in some other ways as well. I have not yet been able to find out where the division lies, and I should like to have that information. What lines of subsidies are being paid by the Department of Agriculture, and why, and what lines are being paid by the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation?

Would the hon. member like an answer now? It would take only a minute. The division is that wherever it is intended to increase production it is done in our department; wherever it is intended to cut down the cost of consumption, it is done in the other department. .

I thank the minister for the explanation, but it seems to me in some cases both principles would apply. Perhaps the division has been made in a way that is suitable to the Minister of Agriculture, if not to both ministers.
The second reason why farmers have enjoyed a modicum of prosperity was outlined by the hon. member who preceded me, namely, that the farmers are finding it impossible to make the necessary repairs on their farms. If one drives through Ontario to-day-I cannot say anything about the other provinces, I do not doubt but that the same conditions prevail-one can see a woeful lack of good buildings and repairs. Because of labour shortages, and because they cannot get materials, farmers have been unable to keep their buildings, fences and machinery in proper repair. They are hoping, now that the war is over, the condition will be changed and they will be able to get more labour and materials. There is only one other thing that they need in the years following the war, namely, an income that will enable them to pay for labour and supplies.
_ Price ceilings were inaugurated three or four years ago. As I understand it, two main reasons were given for that step. The first was to prevent inflation. I do not think anybody will disagree with that. The second was to avoid disastrous slumps and deflation after the war. Something was said at the

time about the deflation and the slump in prices that took place after the first great war. That slump did not occur until two or three years after the war was over. There is no doubt that unless something is done there will be a slump again. The government had evidently forecast that by their announcement on the price of wheat. There is no doubt in my mind at least that if floor prices are to be placed under other classes of farm products on the same basis, using the wheat price as a measuring-stick, the prices that the farmers are to receive for their live stock, dairy products, fruit and vegetables, and all down the line, will not be sufficient to establish a fair relationship between their prices and the prices of goods they have to buy.
May I summarize what I have to say in two or three sentences? The announcement of the government of a floor price for wheat indicates that the government has already embarked on a policy of deflation of farm prices, the policy of lowering prices for agricultural products. It admits that it is powerless to maintain farm prices in the future at levels which will enable agriculture to buy freely and to make the repairs which are so necessary and which have been so long delayed. It also admits that the imposition of price ceilings on agricultural products in the past cannot succeed in preventing deflation of farm prices under peace-time conditions. It further admits that it cannot set prices that will assure the farmer of fair and stable returns and a stable price structure.
I am supporting the amendment which was moved by the hon. member for Souris, because I believe that one situation should be avoided at all costs; unemployment must not be allowed to become general again if it can be avoided. If it is not to be allowed, goods of all kinds must be produced and a market must be found for them at fair prices. The surest way to accomplish this is to maintain the buying power of the primary producer, the farmer, the miner and the fisherman, at substantial levels. To do this I firmly believe that the government must reverse its present policy of deflation as indicated in the statement that the minister made on September 19.

Mr. Speaker, I would not be rising to speak again in this debate had it not been for the introduction of the new amendment and subamendment, and another matter which came up in the house in the last few days. Before speaking to the amendment and the subamendment, I should like to refer to the other matter, which has to do with displaced and stateless persons in Europe.

The Address-Mr. Zaplitny
I wish to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka) and the hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Tucker) in that regard. There are two points that stand out above all the others and I should like to emphasize them while I have the opportunity in this debate. I might say in passing that both these hon. members made a very good case for what they were talking about, and I wish to take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Rosthem on the promotion he has received, as announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to-day. I want to say all the complimentary things I can about the hon. member for Rosthern, because later on I may have something different to say.
The two points I should like to bring out are these. First, it appears evident that a great number of people are scattered throughout Europe who find themselves classified as displaced or stateless. That is, they are being shuffled around from one country to another, and there seems to be some evidence that there is a move afoot to repatriate them forcibly. Now, I believe, and I think hon. members will agree with me on this, that one of the great principles of the Atlantic charter was freedom of choice, or self-determination. In that connection I should like to read article III of the Atlantic charter.
Third, they'-
That is, Mr. Churchill and the Late President Roosevelt.
-respect the right of all peoples to choose the form of government under which they will live; and they wish to see sovereign rights and selfgovernment restored to those who have been forcibly deprived of them.
That is a principle I believe we and all freedom-loving, democratically-minded people can support, and on this basis I make my appeal. I believe the present government, in every way possible, should make its influence felt on behalf of these people, so that they will have freedom of choice and a certain amount of self-determination. I realize that there are difficulties to be overcome; the task is not easy, but on the other hand I believe we should avoid the use of steam-roller tactics in dealing with human beings. Regardless of the country from which they came originally, these are human beings. We know there are people in Europe who for one reason or another do not wish to return to where they lived before the war. I do not want to go into the political implications, because this is not the place for that, but I do want to bring out the humanitarian angle and the fact that if we are to follow the spirit as well
as the letter of the Atlantic charter it will be necessary for us to throw our influence on the side of freedom of choice.
The other point I want to bring out in that connection is the fact that a request, of which I am sure hon. members have received copies, has been made by various Ukrainian organizations across Canada for permission to send direct assistance to their relatives and friends in Europe. I know from personal experience that people who have relatives across the water, whether on the continent or the British isles, are very anxious about their welfare. As an example I should like to remind you of the effort organized by the Kinsmen's clubs during the war to send milk to Britain. For this purpose they established a fund, to which many people cheerfully donated. This milk was used to supplement the assistance being sent through regular channels such as the Red Cross, UNRRA and so on. In this country we have approximately 300,000 people of Ukrainian origin, practically all of whom have relatives living on the continent of Europe. Though I am Canadian born I too have relatives across the water, and I am sure hon. members will appreciate our motives when we ask for permission to send direct assistance to our relatives or those with whom we are acquainted, whose situation we understand, in order to supplement the assistance being provided through regular channels. The request is not made because we have no confidence in UNRRA or the Red Cross; it is only because we feel that in a direct personal way we can assist these bodies which are doing such great work. I hope when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) makes his visit to Europe he will take full advantage of the opportunity to find out everything he can in regard to these displaced persons, so that when he returns the government will be in a position to make some comprehensive statement of policy to guide this house in any future action we may take in that respect.
I should like now to refer for a few moments-and I am going to be brief, because I realize that this debate has gone on for a long time-to the amendment and the subamendment. We are asked by the Progressive Conservative group to accept an amendment asking for ninety per cent of parity.
At least.

I accept that correction; at least ninety per cent. Listening yesterday to the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) speaking to this amendment, I was impressed by the very good case he made, particularly when I realized what a poor case he started with. I rather admired the hon.
The Address-Mr. Zaplitny

member's ability; and what I say about his case is not in any way disparaging to his effort. But he got himself into a curious position. In the first half of his speech he dealt with the removal of controls. He was pretty vehement and decisive about it, and expressed his determination that controls should be removed as quickly and to as great an extent as possible. Then, lo and behold, in the second half of his speech he asked us to accept the principle of parity prices, or at least ninety per cent of parity, which as everyone realizes would entail a great deal of price control. How are we going to remove controls on the one hand and impose or retain controls on the other? At the moment I do not quite see how this can be done. Perhaps at some future time we will have an explanation of that position.
Another question which to my surprise was not dealt with by hon. members to my right in speaking to the amendment is their position on the matter of the grain exchange. As was pointed out by my colleagues here, this question is important. We are definitely of the opinion, and have so stated repeatedly, that our wheat should be handled through the wheat board; we do not want the grain exchange to get its fingers into the pie again. On this point, however, we have not heard an expression of opinion from those to my right. When a group ask the house to vote for an amendment, in effect they ask us to endorse their stand on a certain question. Until we know what that stand is, it seems a risky matter to vote for it. I hope before the vote is taken they will take advantage of this opportunity to tell us just where they stand on the question of the grain exchange.
Another curious thing developed in connection with the amendment, and I should like to bring it to the attention of the house. After the hon. member for Souris, who incidentally is from the same province as myself, introduced his amendment, he was challenged by my colleague the hon. member for Mel-fort (Mr. Wright) as to who had drawn up the amendment. That is quite right, and I am not quarrelling with the hon. member's
{Mr. Zaplitny.]

You will find out.
Apparently the hon. member has not read Hansard for the last five sessions. If he had, he would have seen my complaints each year.

stand consistently, I congratulate him upon it. If they ever come to the point where they have to dissolve that marriage, I hope they will not bring their divorce bill before this house.
When I began speaking I promised I would not take much time, and I shall live up to my promise. In all sincerity I hope hon. members who have the welfare of farmers at heart will vote for the subamendment as a matter of principle.

Several hon. members in the group to my left have said that they do not understand what parity is, and how the mechanics of it might operate.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Who does?

In view of some of the statements made by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, before I can vote conscientiously for the subamendment either he or his leader will have to explain to me how under the wheat board, which they suggest should be continued, they could pay the producer at point of delivery 100 per cent of parity, operate for that crop year, export wheat to every country in the world, sell wheat to millers for domestic purposes, with all the ramifications found in connection with the wheat board, and wind up at the end of the year with the same figure as they paid the producer at the point of delivery. Can they explain what is meant by 100 per cent parity to-day? I have no faith that they can do so.
I pointed out in moving my amendment that we urged a floor price of ninety per cent parity as a result of our studies in the country to the south of us, where they have made a very good job of handling the situation by giving their producers during the post-war years a guarantee of ninety per cent parity, and netted to producers thirty to fifty'' per cent more for their products.
We hear so much theory from the group to my left. One of them asks: If you had 100 per cent parity paid to the producer, where would the money come from? Where does the money come from to pay on the participation certificate?
As to the suggestion that my amendment was drafted by the Toronto members, let me say that we are certainly all agreed in principle, and I think the hon. member's innuendo was unbecoming. Let me tell him that I have far

The Address-Mr. Ross (Souris)
more faith in the Toronto members, the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris), the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol)-
And all points west.

I have more faith in all the Toronto members being desirous of helping the producers to procure parity than I have in the group to my left. Let me tell them that this terrible Tory' government at Toronto which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) spoke of as being one of the few left in the world to-day did more for humanity in its first year of office than the socialistic Saskatchewan government have done in one year and a half. I know how much concerned I was during the drought years to see that the children of Manitoba should have a chance to get primary education. I felt that the province, or the state should assume more responsibility in that respect, and I am glad to say that the so-called Tory government at Toronto in their first year in office undertook to pay fifty per cent of all the costs of education in the province of Ontario and they have carried that out. Contrast that with the false promises of the premier of Saskatchewan. He promised to abolish the educational tax of two per cent on the cost of living and production, but that tax has not been abolished. They have actually added in taxation to the cost of living and the cost of production in that province, and so I ask hon. members in which party they would put their faith. Until somebody' can tell us how the mechanics of this thing can be worked out-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Where do you stand on the grain exchange.

My hon. friend was a member of the last parliament, and he is not so dumb either. In the last parliament the then hon. member for Qu'Appelle, Mr. Perley, and myself moved a resolution asking that the Winnipeg grain exchange be closed. That was before the government had taken action. By the way, let me say that some of my finest friends personally are members of the Winnipeg grain exchange.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is in my constituency.

Then the hon. member had better be careful. My hon. friend made the statement in the house the other day that the ramifications of the Winnipeg grain exchange had been investigated by royal commissions, and they always gave tne grain exchange a clean bill of health in the handling of the wheat of this country. When the Turgeon grain commission made its investigation it reported that in its opinion the exchange could render no useful service during wartime.
I did want to clear up some of this misunderstanding, misinterpretation and misquotation on the part of certain hon. members. I do not see why there should be any misunderstanding, for the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), who is a very able farmer, apparently understood what I meant by a floor price of ninety per cent parity, as hon. members will see if they will re-read his speech. Surely hon. members who professed not to know what parity meant would not be doing that just for political expediency! But several members, including the hon. member who has just sat down, have said that they did not know what parity was, or what the figures were. There was hardly a session of the last parliament when I did not have a run-in with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) over getting parity prices for agriculture. The government took the period 1926-1929
We did not take that. The farm federation took it.

I am not talking about the farm federation or about agriculture at this moment. I was going on to say that the period 1926-1929 was taken by the government as a basis for industry and organized labour, and therefore I argued that probably the same thing should be done for agriculture. If that were done, the parity price of wheat would be $1.42 a bushel, and ninety per cent of that would be $1.28 a bushel, which is three cents above the price which the hon. member for Melfort asked for on September 20, five days before he moved his subamendment.
As I pointed out the other day, the cost of living and the cost of production have risen probably twenty per cent during the war. Certainly that is, true of the farmer's cost of living and the cost of his implements. So, that, if we add twenty per cent to that figure of $1.42, we get $1.70 a bushel, and ninety per cent of that would be $1.53. Therefore, if you take the same period as was taken for industry and organized labour, ninety oer cent of parity either then or now would mean a higher price than the hon. member for Melfort asked for in his speech on September 20.
I have never in my life made any rash promises in either municipal or political affairs in order to gain office. I have never promised anything that I did not believe I could conscientiously carry out if elected to office, and unless the members to my left who have
The Address-Mr. Hansell
COMMONS moved the subamendment have some idea how it could be put into force if carried, I think it should be withdrawn. I have given a great deal of study to this question over the past few years, and I will be bold enough to say that there is a lot about it that I do not know. But I do know what is practical in this country and in the United States, and it is because the subamendment that has been moved by my hon. friends to my left is not practical that I ask the house to vote against it and to vote for the amendment which I have moved, which is practical, and which will guarantee to the farmers ninety per cent of parity at point of delivery, and we will hope for the other ten per cent after the year's operation. I think I have cleared up the various points that have arisen in the debate, and again I appeal to every member of the house to vote for something practical and workable by voting for my amendment. Then we shall have a better understanding of the mechanics of this thing after a year of operation.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in this debate, and I do not now propose to participate in any discussion of these amendments or the technical means whereby, if passed, they may be put into operation. I rise to bring to the house another thought. Personally I have no particular objections to either of the amendments, because I believe each of them aims at an objective which, in general terms, is a square deal for the farmer with respect to the prices of his products. But what I wish to say is this. Our Conservative friends, through the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross), proposed an amendment. I am not going to read it, but it was presented on the basis of an announcement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon). When the hon. member moved his amendment I said to myself, that amendment is reasonable; it is safe; it is sane; it attempts to attain a certain objective and I regard it as desirable. But I find there is one group in the house that evidently does not agree with me on that, for they suddenly decide to go one better than the first amendment, with the result that the house has been subjected to a discussion and drawn into a sort of political race whereby one political party is trying to outbid another.
We heard the announcement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon; we know that we are living in serious times. Personally I do not think that at the present time it graces this house to make motions or amendments which have a 
lot of political significance to them. Perhaps my friends will not agree with that view, but I have the floor and I am expressing my opinion.
I cannot see anything wrong with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Souris. He is not saying that the farmers should not get 100 per cent parity; he is simply asserting that there should be floor prices for all basic agricultural products at levels not less than ninety per cent of parity. They may go higher, and he is not saying that they should not. So that to my view the amendment is most reasonable. Turning over in my mind the reason for this going-one-better stunt, I am reminded that an election is being fought in the province of Manitoba.
When?

It is being fought right now. Some hon. members are out there, campaigning, and I am just wondering whether this second amendment is not an attempt to initiate, here in this house, the Manitoba provincial election.
Why, then, not ascribe the same purpose to the previous amendment?

Well, maybe you can. I am not suggesting that both parties have not the right to move amendments; certainly they have. What I am saying is this, is the first amendment a reasonable one? Is it aimed to reach a certain objective? Is anybody going to complain if in the process the objective is reached or the farmer gets even more than the proposed amendment claims for him? All I am saying is that the amendment is reasonable, and I think the house, particularly the opposition, would be in a much stronger position to persuade the government to act along this line if they had looked at the matter on the basis of its value and its objective. Surely there is not a single member in this house who will contend that the farmer should get one cent less than is coming to him, for that is only reasonable; it is only common sense. Surely my Conservative friends are not putting on an amendment which expresses the view that they want the farmer to get only so much and no more. No man with any common sense would do such a thing. My plea is simply that if we want to bring influence to bear on the government let us get together on something which is practicable and desirable instead of splitting forces. The hon. member for Souris has said, why all this confusion? Apparently it is because it is desired to embark on a little political huffing at one another instead of getting down to practical terms. He has said, let us get down

The Address-Mr. Hansell
to practical things. Well, we will, when we leave politics out of the picture. But just as soon as you bring political sparring into the picture you can throw practical things out of the window.

of privilege, the hon. member is imputing motives and so, I think, is out of order, and I would ask you to have him withdraw those imputations.
No.

Speaking to the point of

What does "politics" mean, Mr. Speaker? It has been defined by Aristotle, a famous Greek, who wrote a learned treatise on the subject. He told us that politics was the science of government; and in speaking as he did, the hon. member for Macleod, if he attributed any motive to the hon. gentlemen who moved the motion, insinuated that the mover and the seconder were both imbued with the science of government, which is politics. The Address-Mr. Low

I am always willing to withdraw anything that is offensive. That is already being said in this country. Well, let us nail that lie to the wall, if it is a lie. I am not going to imply by that that my C.C.F. friends do not want to give the farmers a square deal. Of course they do. I would be a fool to stand here and say that they did not and I am not saying that. But I am saying that in principle I cannot see any difference between the two amendments.
Ten per cent.

No, there is not ten per cent because we have mention of a floor price and it can go higher than that. Therefore I think it is splitting hairs, to say the least, and it tends toward dividing us when we should be united. We in this group have to vote for one amendment or the other, or both. I am going to vote for both, as far as I am concerned. Another thing, when we talk about politics, will any party guarantee that this very debate, these very amendments will not be brought into the discussion in the Manitoba election? Certainly not; they will not guarantee that. If there is any tiny little thread they can reach out for and grasp, making great political capital of it, believe me they will do so. That is politics.
In Manitoba and British Columbia now, but not in the house.

I have said enough, and I object to anything that may happen in this house at any time-I am not imputing motives now-whereby any parties try to gain po'itical advantage by these processes. Times are serious; believe me they are. I do not agree very often with the Prime Minister, but I will agree that he has a tremendous burden upon his shoulders to-day. Let us therefore look at things in a practical manner and attempt to solve in a practical way the problems that face the country.

Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): Just before the question is put I feel that I should say a word on the amendments now before the house. I promise, Mr. Speaker, that I shall not delay the house for more than a minute or two. Further I promise that I shall not follow at least one example already set in this debate, that of making a sneak attack on any hon. member or members who have already delivered a speech or made an interjection.
Yesterday the hon. member for Melfori (Mr. Wright), speaking in support of the C.C.F. subamendment, attacked the Conservative amendment on the ground that it only guarantees ninety per cent, or calls for the guarantee of ninety per cent of the cost of production. I have looked over the hon. member's speech very carefully; I have read the amendment most carefully, and thus far I have been unable to find anywhere in the amendment or in the speech of the hon. member for Souris any reference to cost. The ninety per cent refers to parity of price, which includes profits of all corporations. Surely the hon. members of the C.C.F. are not going to argue that ninety per cent of parity, which includes all profits in addition to all costs, is less than 100 per cent of the cost of production. If they are, Mr. Speaker, then. why are they constantly saying that profits are more than ten per cent? I contend that if the farmers get at least ninety per cent of parity, as called for in the Conservative amendment, they will receive thereby more than 100 per cent of the cost of production.
In neither amendment do I find so much as a hint of the procedure by which those moving the amendments would give effect to the policy which is advocated. Therefore it seems to me that both are straight resolutions of objectives, and objectives only, and I feel quite sure, that no one in any party in this house could conscientiously disagree with the idea of so ordering our Canadian affairs that farmers everywhere in Canada might be able to obtain their fair share of the national income. Of course, the Liberals and the Liberal government are in a different position from the rest of us. They have to worry about where the money is to come from. That is quite a considerable worry in the light of the many things that they have already committed themselves to do under all the restrictions of our present financial arrangement, and my sympathies are with them too.
Since we are considering a straight matter of objectives, and not methods, the Social Credit group find themselves in sympathy

oil
The Address-Mr. Pouliot
with the C.C.F. objectives. We also find ourselves favourable to the objective of the Conservatives, because they are the same in the end. If, on the other hand, the C.C.F. amendment proposes any more socialism than we now suffer in Canada, then this group could not possibly vote for it, but I fail to see that there is any such suggestion. If the Conservative amendment proposes to add to the already effective burden of debt and/or taxation, then the Social Credit group could not possibly vote for it. Whether any group in this house could ever do all that we want with respect to parity of income for the farmers depends upon what method or technique they intend to apply. In my judgment there is simply no possibility that either of the parties who have moved the subamendment and the amendment now before the house can accomplish this most worthy motive without using the procedure that Social Crediters on numerous occasions have so ably, and I would say, so comprehensively placed before this parliament in times past. In the circumstances the Social Credit group will vote for the subamendment. If that fails to carry, then we shall vote for the amendment. By so doing I want it definitely understood that we are taking two opportunities of indicating our unqualified support of the principle of parity of income for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not speak at great length on this subamendment which reads as follows:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that immediate consideration should be given to the establishing of floor prices for all basic agricultural products at parity with other services and products.
All this may be all right theoretically. I am not a statistician, and I am not a farmer, but I live among farmers and I know their troubles. I know that one of their troubles now, and perhaps the worst of all, is lack of man-power on the farms. That is the reason why they have less facilities for transportation and less facilities to cultivate the soil, to harvest, and so on. Therefore, the man-power problem is the most acute on the farm at the present time. I remember, sir, during the early days of the last parliament when a handful of hon. members defended the farmer. We tried to show the importance of the work of the farmer in the war effort. We were not numerous; we were just a small number of members of parliament, and we were looked upon as traitors. I myself was called a friend of Hitler by a Tory member just because I was defending the farmer and trying to rehabilitate him in the minds of our fellow citizens, trying to
show that the farmer in cultivating his soil and working on his farm was doing his duty as a good Canadian citizen during the war. Moreover, I established clearly, as did other hon. members, that without the farmer the soldier would have gone nowhere. Well, sir, it is an elementary principle that cannot be denied by anyone. Now that we hear some speeches about leadership, my suggestion is that we should start by primary education.
Some hon. members remind me of those who know how to read by the euphonic method without knowing their alphabet. I know of a girl who works downstairs on the members* stenographic staff. Mr. Speaker, before the dinner recess I was mentioning what was done to clear up the files at the office of the registrar and the mobilization board in Quebec city. But something else was done by other members of this house. Every time a vote was called for the defence of the rights of the farmers and for the defence of the rights of all those who were engaged in industrial labour, the number of these patriotic members who voted for the defence of those rights varied from five or six to forty or fifty; and most of those who voted for their defence were Liberals, except on a very few occasions.
But something else was done, and it was done by the member for Temiscouata, with the assistance, -help, guidance, support and influence of the late minister of justice, the Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe. That is, I secured amendments to the mobilization regulations,
FMr. Pouliot.]
which were called at first the national resources mobilization regulations-a very long name.
At the start the draftees were called up for one month, and they were told that they would have to serve for only one month. The postponement at that time was for four months only. When the period of training was extended to four months I succeeded in having the regulations amended to provide for a postponement of six months. Afterwards, when the four months training was extended to the duration of the war I succeeded in having the postponement extended according to pleasure, until further notice. That was something. Every time Colonel Ralston tried to turn the screw to make it tighter, I turned it to the other side to make it looser.
During the last election campaign I stated over the radio from powerful stations like CKAC, La Presse, Montreal, and other stations in Quebec city and elsewhere that I had succeeded in securing from the Liberal government recognition of the rights and privileges of the farmer by vindicating his honour, something I never could have secured from any other party or group, and the more so because the Prime Minister had had the skill and ability and finesse to discard his three former war ministers. I stated over the radio -and that broadcast was listened to throughout the province of Quebec-that I supported the Prime Minister inasmuch as he was willing to continue his cleaning of the Liberal party and get rid of all those of the same political tendencies. Here is what was done by a member of parliament, not only for the farmers of his constituency, not only for the farmers of the district of Quebec, not only for the farmers of the province of Quebec, but for all the farmers of Canada-for the farmers of the constituency of my hon. friend the member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) who has just moved his amendment, just as much as for the farmers of Hastings-Peterborough and other places whence came untrue and unworthy denunciations of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I am from the province of Quebec. I am a French Canadian and I am proud of it. I will tell you that I have resented deeply the insinuations and the calumnies hurled against my province by some hon. gentlemen in this house. It was unworthy of them and unworthy of this chamber, and when I think of that going on all during the long years of the war I think also of how few stood up for the defence of the rights of the farmer. Only a handful-one handful, not two handfuls, although occasionally there were

The Address-Mr. Pouliot
two handfuls, but that was all, and we did it because whatever might be the name of the political affiliation of those who did it we were liberal-minded. A Liberal is a man who is a lover of liberty, liberty not only for himself but for others also, and all those who defended the cause of the farmer, the cause of the labourer, the cause of the underdog did so because they were liberal at heart.
I had no political motive in defending the rights of the farmer. My idea was to defend the rights of those whom I have learned to respect since my very childhood. I remember my father's friends who came to our home to see him when I was just a little child and the respect that I was taught to have for them because they were those who fed us at all times. If it had not been for what we had done, despite the insults and humiliations that we have received from a small number of members, especially of the Tory party, and from the mover of the motion, who acknowledged the truth of my denunciation this afternoon, we would have had famine in this country, and my hon. friend the mover of this motion, who wants the farmer to sell his produce at a good price, would have starved because he would have been unable to get any help on his farm. people in. a new election. I am sure the people expect of their members of parliament; the people of every constituency expect of their member, the most earnest and faithful contribution to a solution of the pressing after-war problems that face this nation.
To the motion of thanks five amendments have been proposed. Three have been defeated and two are still before the house. I imagine it would be possible, going through the various departments, to frame five more amendments that would occupy another twenty days of debate. The procedure in the British parliament is that a few of the leaders speak on the motion to adopt the king's address and this occupies usually only two or three days. We have drifted into the practice of moving amendment after amendment, reaching the climax this year in the number of amendments and subamendments that have been proposed.
It is interesting in this connection to note the comments in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms. In the third edition, section 226, at page 95, we read as follows:
It is a mistake to believe that the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne allows members to raise all kinds of issues on the mere ground that they relate to the general situation of the country. In the times of Sir John A. Macdonald and Hon. Alexander McKenzie, considerable restriction was placed on that debate. Speaking on the address in the session of 1875, Sir John A. Macdonald expressed the following opinion: "The practice of discussing the speech from the throne at great length and of raising endless isues upon it was simply an obstruction to business. It was his opinion that, unless the opposition were in a position to move a vote of want of confidence in the government, which he candidly confessed they were not in a position to do on this occasion, the address should be passed without delay."
Then farther on in the same section I read:
Speaking again on the address in 1879, Sir John A. Macdonald said: "I am glad the opposition have adopted the English modern system -;a very proper one-of passing the address without amendment, and when all the various subjects alluded to in it are dealt with, when the measures proposed are before the house, they and their details can be criticized with a full knowledge and satisfactory explanation with regard to the policy of the government."
