cooperation at all times. Your authority goes beyond the membership on the floor to the thousands of visitors in the gallery during the session. We are always delighted to see so many young people in attendance showing their interest in the affairs of government. I should like to speak a word for the ladies who attend in such large numbers. There seems to be a regulation that the officers may admit only those with heads covered. Those who arrive without hats are refused admittance until they deck themselves with boy friend's scarf or hubby's pocket-handkerchief. Surely in these days of artistic coiffures, of modern beauty parlours, we can dispense with this senseless regulation.
The chief point of my remarks in this debate to-day is that just as new methods were employed during the war, which has just terminated, so should we endeavour in this parliament to find new methods of improving our procedure. The service people have been living in a new world; they have travelled across the country, across the prairies and through the mountains in tens of thousands. In hundreds of thousand they have crossed to Great Britain and the continent. They have visited the people of other lands. They have been in charge of and dependent upon machines of destruction devised by our best engineers and scientists. They have been living in a new world, and I am sure there is no person who has served in the forces but has come back with some new thought, new ambitions and new hope. From them, I imagine, come the hope and the prayer for the fulfilment of the prophecy of old, "I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away." While clinging to the old we ought also to be receptive to Changes that will promote our efficiency. These times are a challenge to us to get as quickly as possible to essential things and not to waste time on generalities. There is much in this system that we should retain; perhaps there is some of it that should be discarded or improved in places. Private members have a greater responsibility than that simply of voting, and I think as the responsibility of private members is increased we may find a decrease in that much criticized bureaucracy of which we are hearing these days. Therefore I would urge the government to endeavour to utilize the service of private members to every possible degree.
For the benefit of hon. members who have come to this house for the first time I might state that during the session of 1944 a committee was set up to consider the possibility of amending and improving the standing orders of the House of Commons. This committee

The Address-Mr. Gladstone
made a report, a copy of which I have in my hand. It came before parliament, and much time was given to debating the preamble which preceded the definite recommendations. There was so much tension about certain features of the preamble that the whole recommendation was talked out on that day and finally lost its place entirely.
What should have happened is that opportunity should have been given to hon. members to consider the definite amendments that were proposed in the report of the committee. To illustrate, I might quote the comment on standing order No. 37. Standing order 37 reads as follows:
No member except the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition, or a minister moving a government order and the member speaking in reply immediately after such minister, or a member making a motion of "no confidence" in the government and a minister replying thereto, shall speak for more than forty minutes at a time in any debate.
The comment of the committee in connection with this standing order, reads as follows:
When Mr. Speaker is in the chair, a member can only speak once, but there is no limit to the times of speaking when the house is in committee. Under the present rule, a member may make two or three forty-minute speeches during a sitting of the committee which does not last longer than three hours at a time. This amendment provides for a more equitable apportionment of time and allows more members to take part in the discussions.
The proposed amendment of the committee reads:
Provided always that in the committees of the whole, supply or ways and means, no member shall speak more than once on a particular motion, clause or item under consideration, and not more than twenty minutes continuously, but his right to ask questions relating to the subject matter of the said motion, clause or item under consideration shall not be thereby restricted.
The effect of a change of this kind in standing order 37 would not necessarily mean that during a session hon. members would have less opportunity to speak. Rather I think it would result in more subjects being brought up for consideration and in the resolutions of private members having a greater opportunity of being debated, while in general there would be greater opportunity for all hon. members to participate in discussions. My suggestion is that the report of the special committee of last year should be brought to the attention of this parliament by some means or other. Many hon. members have served during the last ten years, and I am sure they have the feeling that some of the suggested changes, although perhaps not all, would be beneficial. I am also sure that after the new members have been here for two or three sessions they, too,
will be in agreement with some of the proposed changes. So that I trust the government will find some means of bringing these recommendations up for consideration this year.
Another result of the reduction in the length of time a member is permitted to speak would be that it might be possible to shorten the sessions of this house. I am sure many hon. members feel that when we sit until eleven o'clock it makes a pretty long day, since I judge that most members of parliament work upwards of fourteen hours a day, taking into consideration office work, committee work, and listening to speeches in this house for six hours. Therefore I suggest that the government might consider a proposal to conclude a day's sitting at ten o'clock, instead of eleven. In doing so, we would be giving consideration to the faithful members of the press gallery, who send the news of this parliament to newspapers across the country; for when we continue our sessions until eleven o'clock, I am sure their work goes on into the small hours of morning.
There are many things I should like to mention, but I shall confine my remarks to only one or two points in order to hasten the conclusion of this debate. We are gratified to learn that during this month some fifty thousand members of the armed forces will have been returned to Canada. In this connection I should like to pay tribute to the three departments of defence, to the Department of Transport, to the management of the railways and to the railway employees for the arrangements made to look after returning troops. I have come in contact with a number of men who have returned, and they all speak enthusiastically of the consideration they have received on arriving at Halifax or Quebec. It has been a delight to them to be placed in comfortable sleeping cars, and to be served such splendid meals. I am sure we are all glad that such excellent arrangements have been made for the reception of the men and women of our armed services as they return to Canada.
This country has been prosperous during the last five years. Leaving out of the picture the sorrow that has come to many homes, I am sure most of our people are enjoying such prosperity as they had not known for many years previously. As a result, the number of marriages has increased and many new homes have been set up, which is a matter of gratification to all of us. The effects of the family allowance are already being felt. Testimony is coming in to indicate that the sale of milk,

The Address-Mr. Gladstone
for example, has increased. From some of our schoolteachers I have heard that they have noticed their children wearing better suits and dresses, and many children wearing sweaters where they had none before. But in addition to money the children of our country need direction. We must give thanks to many public-spirited people who give leadership in sports and who in other ways are influences for good, but many people are endeavouring to make money out of influences that are questionable. We must stop the commercialization that lowers the moral stamina of our young people. I believe the nerve-wracking pictures our children see at the cinema and on magazine covers have a bad effect. One newsdealer said to me, "I can sell good detective stories without requiring the books to have covers which encourage children to flourish revolvers or daggers."
Mr. Speaker, we must move to protect Canadian homes against the undermining influence of those who seek to make money, regardless of the harm they do to the rising generation. We should feel alarm at the increasing number of divorce cases. I can understand how ill-mated persons just cannot live together. In such cases I favour one divorce, but not a second or a third.
The great offenders, so far as example is concerned, and so far as their influence on the sanctity of our homes is concerned, are the moving-picture actors and actresses. Canada can well afford to be generous to such people in the matter of holidays. Through our customs branch, in the event of their having second divorces, their films should be barred for one year; and for a third divorce a holiday of two years should be imposed. For the sake of our children, Canada must discourage the growing tendency to break up our homes.
We have provided old age pensions at seventy years, and we are now proposing to increase the payments and to modify the requirements. We give benefits to the blind at forty years. Investigators in connection with old age pensions and mothers allowances find many pitiful cases of persons suffering infirmities, and bed-ridden without hope. I suggest that these people should be made eligible at the age of forty years for the benefits of old age pensions.
Canada has gone a considerable distance toward providing more security for our people. However, there is still one great need. Many people have the benefits of superannuation and pension, and among these would be included such groups as civil servants, railway employees, bankers and many others. But all too often we find that the

man who has toiled throughout his best days in a factory is turned out, with no provision for his later years, when he reaches that time in life when his earning power has been depleted. In addition to these, we know of those terrible cases where homes carrying small mortgages are threatened when sickness overtakes members of the families in those homes. Possibly a home must be mortgaged in order to provide proper medical and hospital care for a mother and child afflicted. Very often the result is that that home is never again properly established. Therefore one matter which requires our earnest consideration is that of working out some provision to give security to the homes of so-called common people on those occasions when they require medical and hospital treatment.
I wonder how many Canadians realize the complex considerations of government, those considerations which enter into our dealings with other nations and which have to do with our internal operations. Many things must be purchased from other nations while, on the other hand, we have many other things in surplus quantities which we desire to sell to those nations. We must pay in money that has a recognized value in goods. And so, when the need is created we have a further problem of exchange. Without that exchange problem, with our country operating independently, we might organize our own internal money system pretty much to suit ourselves. We might go on printing money and issuing bonds to an extent where such issues might become voluminous. Then, possibly some group holding radical views might assume power and would scrap all those assets, in order to start over again.
This would not be the method of the people in a free and fairly organized democracy. So I say that our government has many complex problems to deal with. It is reasonably easy and simple to make suggestions calling for expenditures of large sums of money, but it is an altogether different matter to keep everything in balance so as to be fair to all groups in the country and to keep our economy on a solvent basis.
We have been most fortunate in our Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). I am sure all groups in the house will recognize his success in preventing soaring prices during war time. He has our congratulations, and he has our sympathy to-day as he continues his struggle against inflation which he feels, and we feel, would bring such terrible suffering to those with moderate, fixed incomes.

The Address-Mr. Bracken
We can also be grateful that during the war we have had in charge of our munitions programme one who had a first-class engineering training, one with exceptional executive ability, and who possesses a spirit of confidence and optimism. That spirit of optimism was never better displayed by the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) than on the occasion when he was torpedoed in mid-Atlantic. I am sure he will continue to display that spirit of confidence in the house, and in his work as Minister of Reconstruction, despite the attempted torpedoings which ma}' come his way from many of those who would criticize unduly.
In conclusion, may I pay tribute to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I am sure that even among his opponents there is an undercurrent of very warm feeling for the wonderful service he has rendered during the trying days of the war. I believe, too, that most people in Canada have a great deal of confidence in him and in his ability to render service in many ways to other nations of the world as, in joint effort, they attempt to ensure that war shall not come again.

Mr. Speaker, we have before us an amendment and a subamendment. I wish that the members of the house could all support the subaimendment, because I believe it places very simply before parliament what many of us feel should be done, namely, the giving of direct instructions to the government to consider immediately the bringing in of parity prices for farm products.
We have .moved that subamendment because we do not like the language of the amendment. I still feel that there is in it phraseology which does cause some misunderstanding. We were told by a former leader of the opposition in this house, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, on many occasions and at some length, that the written word always prevails. If you take the written word of the amendment it does give rise to the interpretation that was placed upon it by my hon. friend the member for Melfort (Mr. Wright).
As I say, I wish the house could support the subamendment, which is simple, which does not suggest ninety per cent of parity but suggests parity itself. But if the house does not do that, I believe that the amendment offers something better than the principle which is being followed by the government, and if our subamendment is not carried we shall support the amendment.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to speak on the subject of the wheat price policy announced a week or so ago by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) on behalf of the government.
During the course of this debate there has been a good deal of misunderstanding, if not misrepresentation, with respect to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) and with respect to our general position on agricultural prices. I should like to take this opportunity of making clear our position on both.
Before I proceed further, may I take this opportunity of complimenting the leader of the C.C.F. party to my left upon helping to clarify to a small extent the intent of his party which moved an amendment to the amendment because I do not read the same meaning into his party's amendment as evidently he intends should be read.
All I wish to do to-night is to make clear exactly where we stand with respect to the wheat price policy announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and perhaps at the same time make clear where we stand on the general question of parity or a square deal for agriculture.
It is three weeks now since parliament convened. At the opening of the session there was read to us a speech from the throne, which is supposed to outline the government's policy for the session and for the near future. That speech from the throne contains no reference to a change of policy with respect to wheat prices. Two weeks later, on September 19, the Minister of Trade and Commerce on behalf of the government announced this new policy, a new policy which has two effects: (1) it prevents the price of wheat to the farmer from rising, as he indicated it otherwise would likely do in the near future; and (2) it may let prices drop lower than the present floor price or the initial price of wheat.
Let me say in this connection, Mr. Speaker, that this party brought in its amendment in no sense of small politics. We happen to be the official opposition. I hope I shall never say anything in this house that will be critical personally of any hon. member opposite. I respect them all. I know the load they are carrying.
But we all have our responsibilities, and I know the members of the government will expect us to carry them out. When we see policies like this announced and we think there is a weakness in them, it is our duty to point out the other side. There was no opportunity to discuss this question in the debate on the

The Address-Mr. Bracken

address because we had not then been advised of this change of policy. As I said, it was brought in two weeks after the speech from the throne was made. If this policy had been included in the speech from the throne, it, too, would have been included in the amendment which it was my privilege to move. The implication of this new policy is too far-reaching, too filled with ill-consequence to let it go without discussion or without protest. In my remarks to-night I propose to deal with the facts of the situation as we see them.
The question before us now is this. The hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) has moved an amendment to the government's new policy of reducing the floor price of wheat from SI.25 a bushel, which is now the initial price for wheat, to SI a bushel. His motion was in protest against that reduction.
There is no reduction.

The hon. member's motion was in protest against that reduction to SI, and in its place his amendment proposed giving ninety per cent of parity, which would mean a floor price of $1.28 a bushel instead of the $1 a bushel which the government has now announced. It is a protest against that reduction and suggests a sound policy of arriving at what would be good practice. Instead of the policy announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce the amendment proposes to increase the present price from $1.25 to $1.28. As I go along I will explain the details, since the figures are not in the amendment itself.
First let me review the policy announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce a week ago. The intention was to prevent wheat prices from going up beyond $1.55, and, second, to lower the present floor price, which is now $1.25, to $1-not immediately but for the next five years. I may be asked what is wrong with that policy?
In the first place it asks the wheat growers of Canada to assume a burden that the nation should bear. On a free market, wheat prices would now go up and normally the farmers would get the benefit. But this puts a ceiling price on wheat. The government says: We are going to sell wheat at $1.55 and not higher. They do not let the price go up. Then the government suggests a different floor price policy, which may lead to an unwarranted degree of deflation. When the government brings in a policy saying, we guarantee a floor price of $1 for the next five years, that either means something or means nothing. If it means nothing the government should not have brought it ini; and if it means something

it means that the government is fearful that the price of wheat will some time in the next five years drop to $1 a bushel or less. This country cannot face the possibility of wheat dropping to $1 a bushel or less in the next five years. At a price now of $1.55 that would mean a drop of one-third. If wheat is to drop a third, cheese to drop a third, hogs to drop a third, fruit to drop a third, where is the high national income going to come from?
Let me refer briefly to the remarks of the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) and the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), and I know these hon. gentlemen will realize that there is nothing personal in what I have to say. But I shall have to be critical of some of their statements. I think the hon. member for Rosthern left the impression, I hope not intentionally, that our policy means that we stand for only ninety per cent of the cost of production, ninety per cent of parity, on the price of wheat and other agricultural products. This resolution does not bear that interpretation; that is not our policy, and I want to make that fact clear to-night. We stand no more for having agricultural prices at ninety per cent of parity than they stand for having agricultural prices at sixty-two per cent of parity, because that is all that their policy of $1 a bushel is. The government talk about floor prices in this policy of $1 a bushel. That is only sixty-two per cent of parity. We say it should not be sixty-two per cent; it should be at least ninety per cent, and it should not go below that. Ninety per cent is $1.28, and the government's announced policy is $1.
I now want to say a word about the procedure in bringing this policy to the attention of the house. It does not get one very far to criticize procedure; yet it must be said that it was not good procedure for a democratic assembly. What happened? We met here on September 6 and the government brought down the speech from the throne, which is supposed to announce government policy. But before the speech from the throne has been discussed for two weeks the government brings in a new government policy-a policy not mentioned in the speech from the throne-a policy to be passed as a war-time measure in days of peace, a policy determined upon by the government behind closed doors while the house was in session. That seems to be the normal way of doing things under the present procedure. Then it was brought in here one day without notice, brought in here in a manner which denied members the right to discuss it. It is far that reason that

The Address-Mr. Bracken
this amendment was brought forward one evening when many hon. members thought there might be a vote on this debate.
Let us examine in a little more detail what this policy is. I have under my hand Hansard No. 10, and I shall read at page 289 from the remarks of the minister when he brought in this policy. He said:
I wish to make a brief statement on wheat prices.	.
The second world war has concluded with Canadian wheat producers in a particularly strong marketing position.
He means that prices are going up.
Not only has the general disruption and bad weather reduced production in the w-ar areas, but the Australian and north African crop failures and a small crop in Argentina have left Canada and the United States as the only countries at present having substantial export surpluses of -wheat. This has coincided with the release of pent-up demands in the liberated areas.
In these extraordinary circumstances. Canadian wheat might well command for a limited period very much higher prices in the world market.
Do hon. members get that point?
In these extraordinary circumstances, Canadian wheat might -well command for a limited period very much higher prices in the -world market.
Wheat has been selling recently at $1.55. Even conservative estimaters predict that it will go to $1.90, and some, even higher. These are the conditions under which this crop in a free market is being sold, and the government comes along now and says: We are going to sell this, because we are controlling it, at SI.55, and it cannot go higher. The minister continues:
It is in the interest of Canada and of Canadian wheat growers that the importing countries should continue to obtain Canadian wheat at prices not in excess of those prevailing at the end of hostilities.
He says it is in the interest of Canada, and he goes on:
Accordingly the government, by order in council, has instructed the Canadian wheat board to offer wheat for sale for export overseas at prices not higher than the current export price of $1.55 per bushel.
At the moment I am trying to get the facts before the house. For a dozen years before the war farmers were getting prices much below parity. Everyone will admit that. The last two or three years we have been getting fairly good prices, and now, when the outlook is that they will go higher, we are denied the right to accept higher prices, "in the interest of Canada". Then he goes on:
In asking Canadian producers to forgo such benefits as might be realized in the short run through higher export prices, the government realizes the paramount need for- -

-relative stability of income to wheat producers.
Are the farmers going to get stability of . income by a lowering of the present floor price from $1.25 to $1. And because the government are doing that it thinks it has to give a quid pro quo, and what is it?
Toward this end, the government undertakes that in the five-year period ending July 31, 1950, producers will receive not less than $1 per bushel basis No. 1 northern, in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver on the authorized deliveries for each crop year.
Not for all their wheat, but for the authorized deliveries, whatever that is; a part of the crop. Then he goes on. Listen to this: By providing a long-term floor price of not less than $1 the government will protect producers against the consequences of any sharp reversal in the world wheat position during the next five-year period.
If that means anything, it suggests that they are afraid that the level will be down there or lower. This country cannot contemplate a condition of letting wheat go down to SI or lower in the next five years; with the burden which this government has put upon the people-and many of us support most of those expenditures-that burden cannot be borne if the national income is to be lowered to anything like the degree which is here contemplated- as a possibility. Further: The government, in adopting this policy of a maximum price for overseas shipments for the present and a floor price for five years, is asking the producers, in their own interests, to forgo exceptional short-run advantages in favour of a long-run stability of income.
What kind of stability of income- will wheat at $1 a bushel bring to the farmers? If that sort of deflation is to take place in o-ur whole economy, there is no- chance- in God's world of this government collecting enough taxes from the Canadian people to carry the services they are proposing for the people- of the country. The statement goes on:
Any further increase in wheat prices now would aggravate the problems of economic and political readjustment of the liberated areas to Canada's detriment in future trade with those areas.
I agree with that. I compliment the government on that policy, but I do not compliment it on the policy of leaving the burden on the wheat growers. Then it goes on: There is a moral obligation not to take advantage of our recent allies in their time of compelling need.
A moral obligation- on whom? On the 250.000 farmers or on this nation? Then the
minister states:
I wish to lay on the table copies of order in council P.C. 6122.
The Address-Mr. Bracken

I should like to refer to that order in council for a moment. This is the order in council which the minister tabled on the very day on which it was passed. I will refer to one clause':
That as a further means of stabilizing wheat prices-
Mark these words "stabilizing wheat prices" -by a floor price of $1..
That as a further means of stabilizing wheat prices during the post-war period it is the intention that steps shall be taken to ensure that producers will not at any time up to July 31, 1950, receive less than $1 per bushel . . .
Mr. Speaker, stabilizing wheat by such an action as that is all eyewash. It will not stop a deflation which this country cannot afford if it is to carry the services the government has undertaken to assume.
Perhaps at this point I should deal with the remarks made by the hon member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). I listened with interest to what the hon. gentleman had to say in the first part of his address and I was prepared to compliment him on the nature of it, but I must say I was surprised and disappointed when he came to the last part of that speech. I will not say that the hon. member deliberately misrepresented our position or what was in the amendment, but what he said had the effect of misrepresenting it. Here is what the hon. gentleman said, as reported on page 480 of Hansard, and I quote:
I am surprised that he introduced an amendment which suggested that the farmers of Canada should be satisfied with ninety per cent of their cost of production.
That is not in this amendment, and when that fact was brought to the hon. gentleman's attention he made this statement:
Mr. Wright: Let me read the words of the actual amendment.
And this is what he read; he read only part of the amendment:
. . . immediate consideration should be given to establishing for a period of years floor prices for all basic agricultural products at levels not less than ninety per cent of parity.
As I say, he read part of the amendment. I propose to put on the record the other part so that the house and the Canadian people can read them both together. Here is the first part:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that,-[DOT]
I hope hon. members will listen to this.

pending the establishment of a more stable and equitable price structure for Canadian farm products based on parity of income for farmers,-
Pending that time.
-immediate consideration should be given . . . 
Immediate consideration should be given to the advisability of establishing for a period of years floor prices-not parity prices but floor prices, the thing the minister was talking about-for all basic agricultural products at levels not less than ninety per cent of parity.
The hon. member then went on to say, further down on page 480:
The hon. member now suggests that for a period of years we in agriculture should be satisfied with ninety per cent of our cost of production.
That is not in the resolution and the hon. member for Souris never said that. He was talking about floor prices, the same thing the minister was talking about when he brought in the government's dollar floor price plan. After some discussion on the floor of the house the member for Melfort said this:
That is why I am so surprised that the present amendment should be brought in by the hon. member, because he states we should get not less than ninety per cent.
Mr. Speaker, that is the chief reason why I am speaking to-night. I do not think hon. members wanted to misrepresent our position and I do not want to misrepresent it. I want the house to know what it is. We do not expect to upset the government's policy, but when we see a weakness in that policy we must try to present that weakness; and we hope we can present a united front in trying to get the government to raise the figure from SI to at least $1.28. Then the hon. member for Melfort moved his resolution:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that immediate consideration should be given to the establishing of floor prices for all basic agricultural products at parity with other services and products.
If that means anything in connection with wheat it means that he wanted it established at $1.42, because that is what parity is. I wish to compare that statement of the hon. member for Melfort with the statement he made a few days earlier in the debate. Here are his words as reported on page 330 of Hansard:
I am sure that $1.25 a bushel is the lowest floor price that should be set for wheat in Canada. That is a price which would give to the average producer

I hope that all hon. members are listening to this. I was going to say it pains me as much to read it as I am sure it will pain you in the C.C.F. group to hear it.
That is a price which would give to the average producer a reasonable return for his labour and for the investment which he has in his farm and in his equipment.
The hon. member who moved this amendment. which means, if it means anything, that $1.42 is the floor price, stated only three

The Address-Mr. Bracken
or four days before that that SI.25 would give to the average farmer a reasonable return for his labour and for the investment which he has in his farm and in his equipment.
On a question of privilege-
Sit down.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who is speaking-and I do not often rise in defence of the C.C.F.-made the statement that the hon. member for Melfort deliberately misrepresented-
I did not.
Sit down.
Sit down.
Don't be foolish; he said no such thing.
On a question of privilege, I ask that it be read back.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: That will be more publicity for you.
He distinctly covered that and it is the opposite.
Order. I have listened to the hon. member and I could not detect any question of privilege.
Mr. Speaker, I have been critical of the statements made by the hon. member for Melfort-
You made it.
-but I am sure he will not charge me with saying that I deliberately misrepresented him.
You made it.
Why are you his champion?
Never mind.
You are trying to misrepresent.

I have one other reference to the statement made by the hon. member for Melfort who moved the amendment to the amendment, and then I shall be through with that part of it. To-day in the discussion on a point of order, he said: "All I want is a square deal for farmers." A few days ago he said that $1.25 would be in effect a square deal. His amendment means $1.42, and it means more than that. He is saying that he wants a floor price and he is going to make the parity price-$1.42-a floor price. Then, under our system, where we have floor prices and ceiling prices, presumably in a
time like this when wheat is bringing $1.55 he would get the difference between $1.42 and $1.55, which would be more than a parity.
I am sorry that I have had to take so much time in dealing with his remarks, but I am sure the house will realize that his statement did leave a wrong impression with respect to what our amendment means, and with respect to what we meant it to mean.
I have commented on the way in which the matter of floor prices was brought forward, and I have reviewed the pertinent features of the policy announced by the government. I should now like to examine for a little while more clearly the two main features of this policy. Let me first deal with the prevention of prices going up and then with that of adopting a floor price policy of $1, in place of what is now a floor price policy of $155.
There is one other weakness in the statement. It was not the minister's business to do it, but the statement does not cover all agricultural products. Our amendment was meant to establish the parity principle in the floor price for all agricultural products. In a system where you have floor prices and ceiling prices we contend that the floor price should never be less than ninety per cent of parity for all basic agricultural products.
What is parity?
If the hon. member will hold his patience for a little while he will learn. I would suggest that if he represents an agricultural community it is about time that he knew what it was.
I got elected again.
Order.

We wanted the house to have an opportunity of approving the principle that as long as we have floor prices and ceiling prices, the principle of making floor price should not be lower than ninety per cent of parity.
The reason the government gives for the first of these two policies, is, as has been mentioned before, that it will prevent prices from going up and thereby help to restore the economy of other nations. I do not disagree with that; I only disagree with the policy of asking one section of the Canadian people to bear that burden. What is the reason given for adopting a floor price of $1. The following words appear in the order in council. I ask the house to listen while I quote them: "to protect producers against any sharp reversal of the world wheat position." If that means anything it means that it is expected there is a considerable chance that wheat will go down
The Address-Mr. Bracken

below that figure. For a dozen years before the war we had wheat below $1 a bushel. I am sure there is nobody in this house or in Canada who wants to contemplate a condition in this country with wheat and other agricultural products that low. The government says it is a world responsibility to help other nations to reestablish their economy. With that we all agree, but we do not agree that a section of the Canadian people should bear the burden. Then, as a quid pro quo for preventing prices from going up the government offers this as something worth while. And instead of increasing the present floor price it actually lowers it by twenty per cent, from SI.25 to SI.
In effect what the government is saying to the Canadian farmer is that you lose both ways. Prices will not be allowed to go up, but prices may be allowed to go down to as low as $1. That policy is extremely inadequate and unsatisfactory. It is a sop with no substance either to the farmers or to this nation. That policy is, in my judgment, unsatisfactory, because it will not give a fair deal to growers with SI.42 being parity to-day. You are not likely to get parity if you are going to let the price go down to as low as $1 and stop it at $1.55.
I do not need to tell hon. members the condition of agriculture during the last few years when nearly one-third of our people on farms frequently got only one-sixth of the nation's income and sometimes only one-tenth. This policy will not enable farmers to buy the products of industry. I do not need to tell the house that sometimes in the past the Canadian farmers have received only $400,000,000 in a year. Last year they received $1,700,000,000. They can buy the products of industry if we keep up the prices of agricultural products; they cannot if we do not. This policy will not enable agriculture to help maintain employment. If farmers cannot buy the products of industry, then industry cannot employ people. In the past six years, because nature smiled upon us and because for the last two or three years we have had good prices, the farmers of this country received $6,600,000,000. In the six years prior to that they received only $3,300,000,000; I am using round figures in both cases. With $6,600,000,000 they are able to buy the products of industry and help keep our economy functioning in a healthy manner. But this sort of policy-a $1 floor price-will not enable agriculture to maintain a high national income. I need not tell hon. members that prior to the war the farmers of this country, on the average, if they allowed themselves any interest on their capital, in some years made

only $1 a day, and in no year made more than $3. Even if they did not allow themselves any interest on capital invested the income for the whole farm family was only from $2 to $4 a day.
This sort of policy-low floor prices-will not enable agriculture to keep up production. The price incentive will, as it did during the war. During the last five years an average of seven million tons more of cereals were produced than during the five years immediately before the war. That was partly because nature was good to us, but the principal cause was reasonably fair prices.
Last but not least, this policy does not tend to create confidence on the part of our people. On the other hand it creates lack of confidence in the whole government programme of reconstruction. If they suggest the possibility of wheat going down by one-third, to $1, what are our hog producers going to think; what are our cheese producers going to think; what are our fruit producers going to think; and if agriculture goes down, where is the hope of employment and where is the hope of a high national income? I do not know what the national income is to-day, but a short time ago some people estimated it at around $9,000 million. If that is to be reduced by one-third, to $6,000 million, and this government asks the Canadian people to pay taxes three or four times as high as before the war, they will never be paid. A reduced national income of that kind cannot carry such taxes, and the government's programme will fail.
From what I have said hon. members will gather what I conceive shall be the objective of a policy of this kind. First of all, it should be equity for producers. We ask no more than that; but we ask that much. Another objective should be stability for the industry. You cannot have stability with prices ranging from $1.55 to $1, any more than a wage-earner of this country can have stability if his wages jump around-$155 now and $100 later. If farmers have low incomes they cannot pay the farm wages now demanded. And a high national income is necessary to a high national production.
I had intended to say a good deal more, Mr. Speaker, but I am reminded by one who is close to me that there may not be many conversions after the first three-quarters of an hour. I am not expecting to make many conversions; all I am trying to do is to make our position clear. In connection with this question of parity; in deciding what is a fair relationship between the prices received by farmers and the prices paid by farmers, one of the best guides to-day is the parity principle. By this we mean that the prices for

The Address-Mr. Bracken
what the farmer has to sell should bear a fair relationship to the prices for what he has to buy, and should rise or fall approximately at the same rate as the prices of the goods and services he has to buy. That is equity, nothing more or less. This approximate equality has been taken in the United States from a period when agriculture and the rest of the economy was in reasonable balance. The United States uses the years 1910-14 as the base period. Sufficient data is not available in Canada to make these earlier years a scientific base period. I make the suggestion that the committee on agriculture and colonization or a special committee appointed for the purpose should give some study to the selection of a proper scientific base period for Canada. Pending such action, however, I have taken the period 1926-29 as the most suitable period that can be selected in Canada, at least for certain crops. In the case of wheat the average price of No. 1 northern, Fort William, was $1.34 a bushel for the three months of heavy delivery in the years 1926-29. This spring the official indexes show that the prices of things farmers buy, including production, living, taxes, interest and wages, have risen an average of six per cent above the basic period 1926 to 1929. A fair or parity price for wheat would therefore be six per cent higher than the base period, or $1.42 a bushel.
We believe in the parity principle. In the United States they took a period before the war which they considered to be one in which there was a healthy relationship between the prices of agricultural products and the price= the farmers had to pay, and they use that as the base period. If later the prices the farmer has to pay go up they would see that the prices the farmer received would go up also, and that if the prices the farmer had to pay went down, then the prices of their products would go down also. That is what they regard as the parity price principle. That is the policy we adopted at Winnipeg. But I go further than that. They took that base period only because it was the best thing they could have as a guide. A base period is not always the best guide. That kind of parity does not always give a fair deal to farmers. So that we have adopted the policy that farmers should have their cost of production, and should have on top of that, incomes equal to the average of the incomes of other gainfully employed workers in other occupations.
We believe that the parity principle, using the 1926-29 base for most products, could very well be the basis of setting floor prices for the basic farm products. In order to avoid wide
fluctuation in prices, we believe that until a rigid parity price structure is brought about we should keep floor prices as high as we reasonably can. That is why we ask that the floor price be raised above the government's announced figure.
Then, to skip a good deal of what I had intended to say, may I leave this word with the house. It is clearly evident that what farmers have received in the past is far below parity, at least until the last two or three years. In 1940 and 1941, even after adding the participation payments, they received thirty-eight cents a bushel below parity. In 1942 they received thirty cents less than parity. It is extremely unlikely that the participation payments for 1943 and 1944 will, with the final returns, reach parity.
I am not going to keep the house any longer. As I resume my seat, I wish to say that we stand only for equity for agriculture. Prior to the last several years the price policy of this country was one of letting prices go as low as they chose or as high as they chose. Now, and particularly since this war, the policy of this government-and I have not objected to it-has been to put on a ceiling price beyond which they will not let prices go, and establish a floor down here below which they cannot go. They set it at $1.25 for wheat, and it is that to-day. But with the government's policy it may be $1 in the future.
I believe we shall have greater stability in this country the more we can bring those two figures closer together by raising the floor price and not much stability when the price range is from $1 to $1.55.
When this amendment was prepared, as I [DOT]have said, it was hoped that all hon. members on this side of the house might feel that they could support it. I would not expect that it would gain the support of hon. members on the other side of the house, because I can quite understand that when the government determines upon a policy it is not likely to accept the ideas of the opposition. So that, to speak frankly, we were not expecting 'hon. members opposite to support us.
Our position has been-and to some extent it has been misrepresented-that we want the parity principle established. We do not differ in that respect, on this side of the house. And we want the government's floor price policy of $1 raised to $1.28.
But I do not want hon. members behind me to be misrepresented to their disadvantage. Therefore, I am going to say to my supporters that, having established where we stand on this matter and 'having brought forward a policy which is sane and fair and, I am sure, appeals to all hon. members as a policy
The Address-Mr. Gardiner

that cannot be misunderstood-I am going to say to hon. members behind .me that I shall not object if they choose to support the amendment to the amendment as well as the amendment itself.
