After the discussions with them we retained the wheat acreage reduction payments and we payed ninety cents a bushel as the initial payment.
That remained until 1943, when the initial payment was raised to SI.25 a bushel. I have here on record the statement made by the people of the farm federation following that announcement. They complimented the government upon the action we had taken in making the payment SI.25 a bushel. The only occasion upon which they have used $1.25 a bushel as the floor price in connection with their resolutions was in the present year, when they asked this government to retain the initial payment of $1.25 a bushel for the year 1945-46; and this government has done so. In other words, mot only have we met the wishes of the farm organizations in Canada with regard to a fair price for wheat, but we exceeded them in 1943. When we exceeded them they asked us to continue that advance payment during the following year.
I recall those resolutions only to call the attention of the house to the fact that, while certain hon. members are raising the question as to whether the farmers will be satisfied with this price, farm organizations declared their belief in it before we undertook it, and farm organizations right across the three prairie provinces, as the hon. member for Rosthern indicated last night, expressed themselves as satisfied with the policy which has been adopted by the government.

Mr. Speaker, I think the
Minister of Agriculture is getting slightly mixed. He referred to what the hon. member for "Humboldt" said. I did not speak last night.

I meant the horn, member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker). I was paying the hon. member for Humboldt a compliment he did not deserve. I am glad the hon. member for Humboldt called my attention to it, because I would not want to mislead the people or this house into believing the hon member on this side represents any other seat- than Rosthern.
I was saying a moment ago that they had reasons for passing these resolutions in the farm organizations. Those reasons took them right back to the period of time that I reviewed a few moments ago. Someone said-
I think it was the hon. member for Souris- this afternoon in reply to am hon. member of the C.C.F. group that there had been an

experience with the policy of attempting to make high payments the floor price in connection with wheat. That experience was during the very period of time of which I spoke at the beginning of my speech, when prices of wheat were high. We started in western Canada with a floor price of $1 a bushel under the pool. The farmers were then handling their own pooling of wheat. We held the price at $1 too long. Then we reduced it year by year until finally, I think, we got it down to some seventy cents a bushel. But every year we were reducing it from $1 a bushel down, the wheat pools were taking a loss, and in the end they lost $30 millions and had to come to the government at Ottawa and to the three governments in western. Canada in order to get their position taken care of by using. the finances of the people of this country.
In every discussion I have had with farm leaders in western Canada, when held in places where we can sit down and talk with regard to them without an audience and base our talks on the experiences in the past, they have called attention to the fact which was called attention to this afternoon by the hon. member for Souris, namely, that it is dangerous to have the initial payment higher than is necessary in order to pay the operating costs of the farmers who produce the wheat. They all agree that we should depend upon participation for our profits. I make that statement in order to repeat that the men who passed these resolutions know the wheat business better than anybody else in Canada. The pools are composed of producers growers of the wheat, and 'they marketed in the province of Saskatchewan, which produces more than 50 per cent of the wheat grown in Canada every year. The men who market that great volume of wheat have realized from experience the difficulty of setting floors which are too high in connection with tire product that they handle, because they know we must have the marketing of agricultural products established on a sound economic basis as well as upon a basis which will give us the highest possible returns for our products. They have suggested, in all their resolutions passed with regard to this matter down to the year 1945, that the basic price or initial payment be not less than $1 a bushel.
Having that before us, the government was placed in a position of having to discuss this question recently in the light of the facts as they now exist throughout the world. Wheat has been gradually going up, but wheat is not the only thing which has been gradually going up.

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
This government embarked in 1941 upon a policy of attempting to maintain ceiling prices not only upon those things we have to sell but upon those things we have to buy, and I think I can say without fear of contradiction that the majority of men and women from one end of this country to the other, no matter which party in this house they voted for, believe that that policy, as it has worked out from 1941 to the present time, was in the interests of Canada. Under that policy there was one product upon which no ceiling was set, and that was wheat. Ceilings were set on beef, pork, cheese, butter, and every other processed farm product, but not on wheat, although a ceiling was set on other grain. One reason why a ceiling was not set upon wheat was the fact that wheat was then at seventy-eight cents a bushel. Members from the western part of Canada took the position at that time, as we take it now, that you cannot set up in this country an economy based upon seventy-eight cent wheat, and in taking that position and maintaining it and working for it we established the position that there would not be a ceiling set on wheat at that particular time, and not until it passed parity of $1.42.
What is the result of that? The leader of the opposition has said to-night that in his opinion some of the things which have been suggested in the policy that has been announced are good of themselves but, he says-and I agree with him in this-two hundred and fifty thousand farmers, the producers of wheat in western Canada, should not be called upon to bear the burden of utilizing our wheat in order to assist people in other parts of the world, but that all the people of Canada must do that. As I say, I agree with him on that. What did we do, Mr. Speaker? Back in 1941 we said that every person in Canada-it does not make any difference whether he is a banker on St. James street, a farmer in western Canada, or a labourer in the Ford plant-as long as the controls remain upon prices in Canada, can buy his bread based on seventy-eight cent wheat, and no higher. Well, may I say to my hon. friends that when we raised the guaranteed floor on wheat to $1.25 a bushel we said to every farmer in Canada, you are going to be guaranteed $1.25 a bushel for your wheat delivered at Fort William. At the same time we said to every man, woman and child in the Dominion of Canada, you are going to buy your bread based upon the price of seventy-eight cents for wheat and you are going to buy it there as long as controls last.
I call the attention of the house to the fact that that is placing the burden exactly where it belongs. It puts the burden on the treasury of Canada and through the treasury of Canada upon all the taxpayers of the country, whether farmers, or others.
That is not a new policy. That policy has been in existence since 1941. Well, now, on the other farm products, what was done? The price of meat in 1941, in the four-week period which was established as the basis of price control, the price at which meats sold to consumers was higher than it was in the period of 1926-29. The price of many of the other farm products was higher than it was in the period of 1926-29. What did this government do? We established these higher than 1926 or parity levels as the ceilings I should say, when saying that, that the price of live cattle, the price of hogs, the price of other natural products from the farm, unprocessed, was not so high, on some of them at least, as the average price from 1926 to 1929. The government therefore did this. We set a ceiling upon meat; we set a ceiling upon dairy products; we set a ceiling upon the processed products of different kinds. But we said to the farmer, we are going to allow the prices of the commodities that you sell unprocessed to rise up to the levels provided for under the ceilings that are set on meat and other processed products.
And so from 1941, through that year and the next, these primary farm products and some others, cattle, hogs, cheese, butter, went gradually upward until they all passed the average prices of 1926-29, which is parity, or we added subsidies to make them higher.
The other night the leader of the opposition said that we had not increased the price of hogs in the year, 1944 over 1945, other than to add a $3 premium and a $2 premium to the prices which had been paid after prices on grain had been raised up to the levels I spoke of a few moments ago. I corrected that statement in my speech the other day, and I refer to it again only in order to say this, that the only reason why we stopped with seventy-five cents in raising the price of bacon at Saint John in the winter of 1943-44 was the fact that when we added the seventy-five cents we brought the price of that product up to the ceiling as established in 1941, and so we said that rather than break through the ceiling price upon pork we would submit to a policy of putting a premium on high-grade hogs of $3 and $2 and maintaining the price of hogs at a level which did not break the ceiling on pork as it was established in 1941.
The Address-Mr. Gardiner

There is one thing I cannot understand about the position taken by the leader of the opposition. I opened my remarks the other night with regard to what he had said in the first address with a statement I am going to read again. He says that the reduction in hog production and the going down of production of bacon in 1945 as compared with 1944 is due chiefly to the government's policy of keeping hog prices so far out of line with feed prices as to discourage hog production. Well, to-night he is arguing for the policy of having grain prices higher, while at the same time wheat is the only product which down to the present moment has not had a ceiling upon it; and wheat, as he stated in his previous address, influences the cost of feeds and therefore would influence the cost of producing these bacon products to every farmer in the dominion who produces them.
What I wish to say is this. We cannot, argue both ways on these questions. Feed enters into the production of every live stock product we have; when we argue for a ceiling price in one breath-and every member of the official opposition agrees that ceiling prices have been a good thing-we have to admit that _ these ceiling prices must be held at certain levels throughout certain periods of time; and when they are held on one product they must be held on others if we are to deal equitably with the people of this country.
In dealing with that matter this afternoon the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) raised the question of subsidies, and I made some reference to the fact that we have subsidies on most farm products. We have them put on in two or three different ways, and this brings me back again to the suggestion that all the people of Canada ought to be made to pay, when we bring down policies which result in the giving away of farm products or any other products from this country to the people of some other countries, and not simply one class of the people.
Prices of farm products were not raised in the markets in the manner described by someone this afternoon. We were told that we had to take care, in dealing with this particular question, that we did not create a situation whereby we would lose our markets through raising our prices in the markets of the other countries of the world. I think that statement was made by the leader of the opposition to-night.
It was not the other countries of the world that made these prices. The other countries of the world have been getting assistance under mutual aid, which resulted in our being able to pay our farmers higher returns, and 
that mutual aid came out of the public treasury, a charge on all the people of the country, making it possible for us to pay about the difference between eighty-five shillings and one hundred and thirteen shillings on bacon to farmers through the packing plants for the hogs that were marketed off their farms. A similar condition exists in connection with cheese, in connection with canned milk, in connection with every product that was provided to Britain and other allied countries under the mutual aid arrangement.
Therefore what I want to emphasize in that connection is that in anything we do with regard to ranges of prices on wheat we are not interfering with something which had been established in some other country in recent years during the war. We are dealing with a condition under which this country, under the able leadership of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), raised funds with which we paid for Canadian products, and then we sent those products to other countries, taking back from our allies what they could afford to pay under the conditions then existing, and charging the rest of it up to the billion dollars of mutual aid which this government provided in order to help our allies during the war.
It might be said and they have said it-I do not need to say it; our allies have said it -that Canada has done a worth-while job in that regard in carrying that policy through during the last three or four years of the war, and we believe that by carrying that policy through we have created a situation which will make it possible for us to market the commodities we produce in this country in countries which believe that they owe something to us because of the service we gave in their period of greatest trial. That is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) had in mind when he said in this house the other day that we as a government must give consideration to the effects which any price that may be established for our products at the present time, particularly products we are selling in great volume, have upon the economy of the other allied nations alongside of whom we fought. It is in order that we may maintain the proud position which we hold among the allied nations to-day, of having done everything possible to give service in every way in order to assist in the winning of the war. When we have come to the end of it, it is not our intention to do things which might cause us to destroy the good feeling which we established then.
Let me now touch on the position as it relates to the war period and as it relates

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
to the period before the war and to the future. "We have been struggling with this wheat question not only ever since the war started but since 1932, when the government of the day sent a delegation from Ottawa, which took with them representatives from the three western provinces, to discuss our wheat problem at that time. It was the problem of a great carryover of wheat which we desired to sell in the European markets. At that time there was set up an organization which has been discussing our wheat problems ever since. As I said here the other day, when this wheat question was being discussed by someone, we have not succeeded in getting any definite arrangements entered into by the five great wheat-producing countries of the world in their relationship with the great consuming countries of the world. We have had these people together; we have been discussing their problems and our problems. That has all been helpful, but when it came down to getting definite arrangements as to what the price and the acreage were to be we have always been confronted with some difficulties which have usually resulted in lack of agreement-I would not say in disagreement, but in lack of agreement.
I wish to say to the house to-night that if it is ever possible at any time to lay the records of those discussions, which have been held in camera, before the people of the world, and at the same time before the Canadian people, it will be found that in every case the advances made by this country toward the other countries were in a line which, if they had been agreed to, would have satisfied the demands of farm organizations from one end of Canada to the other. One of those demands has been written down by the farm federation on many occasions. They have said, "What we want is a stabilized price for wheat." They said, "We want it stabilized over a period of years." They have said on occasions, "We want a $1 price established." I remember on one occasion that they were saying in one breath they wanted a price established at $1 and in the other criticizing the government at Ottawa because the government would not sign a proposed agreement presented by this commiittee. I went so far as to say this to them: "If you want us to sign the agreement, which is before us at the present time, with the nations of the world, which you have said in one resolution you want, and you want us to accept the price which is in that agreement as the basic price for wheat, then it is lower than 11 a bushel, and the other countries of the world will not agree to its being higher." That was just prior to the war.
Since the war, these discussions have been changed from London to Washington and they have been going on there. What I wish to say to the house is that policies similar to those which have been advocated by the farmers of western Canada with regard to wheat have been submitted to that organization year by year. What the Minister of Trade and Commerce meant the other day when he answered a question from the other side of the house, and when he stated that these countries recently meeting in London had not agreed, was that they had not agreed to a policy which I am sure would have met with the approval of all the farm organizations in Canada.
When that agreement was not reached this government announced its policy in the house the other day. That policy gives us five more years in which to carry on negotiations. That is why the farm organizations, without any coaching on our part, have gone to the press in their own cities of Calgary, Regina and Winnipeg, and said that they are satisfied with the policy that has been announced. Some of them told us clearly that they want us to go ahead and negotiate other steps and arrangements, but there is no way that you can proceed to negotiate steps and arrangements with governments at the present time and hope for any settlement in time to deal with the next crop, let us say, or probably the next crop or two. You cannot depend upon having absolute settlements made among the great number of nations that are involved in this wheat question, while world conditions are what they are.
Therefore what we have said to the people of this country is, that for the present we have asked the wheat board to sell wheat at not higher than SI .55 a bushel. That was the price the market would have paid for our wheat on the last occasion in which we were dealing with the British government just before the policy was announced. Therefore we have said that we are going to sell wheat to the overseas people-we do not say to anyone else-at SI .55 a bushel for the time being. Then we have said that for the next year, down to the end of July, 1946, the initial payment is exactly what it was asked to be by the farm organizations down to that period of time, namely, $1.25 a bushel. Then we have said that in the meantime we are going to carry on with the same policies in relation to wheat and other farm products as we have been carrying on with from 1941 down to the present. And we say-we have not said this in so many words, but I am sure that every member of the government will agree with me when I say it-there is not any intention on the part of the members of
The Address-Mr. Gardiner

this government, or of any one associated with it, to lower the initial payment on wheat below $1.25 a bushel as long as the wheat of this country can be disposed of anywhere at $1.25 a bushel. We are carrying out the policy at the moment just as the circumstances warrant our carrying it out, namely, guaranteeing a floor price of $1.25 a bushel for this year, no matter what happens, and going on with our negotiations with other people as to what the price ought to be, and saying that for the time being, while we are selling wheat overseas to the countries that need our food, we are going to charge them only $1.55 a bushel for it.
I agree with the leader of the opposition that to the extent that we might have got more we are asking the 250.000 farmers who grow wheat to carry that part of the burden for the time being. And we are asked, what are they getting in return for it? We are saying to them that, no matter what happens during the next five years, we are going to see to it that you never have to take less than $1 a bushel for your wheat, basis Fort William. What does that mean? It means that it does not make any difference where wheat goes on the market, if it goes down to fifty cents a bushel we are going to take the money from all the people of Canada to pay the difference between fifty cents and $1. All we are suggesting to the 250,000 farmers is that, while it is $1.55 or more, and while we have ceiling prices on other commodities in Canada, we are going to ask them to permit us to sell whatever wheat we do sell to our overseas allies at $1.55 a bushel during that time. But at the same time we say to them by inference, if not in words, there will not be any ceiling price on your wheat any longer than ceiling prices remain on other commodities in this country. We did not say there was a ceiling of $1.55 for five years. We said there would never be a floor of less than $1 a bushel for five years; but we have said that as long as wheat is $1.55 or more, and as long as there are ceiling prices on other products in this country, since wheat has gone above parity, to $1.55 instead of $1.42, we are prepared to place a ceiling of $1.55 a bushel on what wheat is sold to our allies.
To-day on the orders of the day someone asked whether the government was giving attention to the possibility that someone might start to sell wheat outside this country, into the United States, at higher prices. In reply to that question I say that all the wheat in Canada is delivered to the wheat board, and the wheat board is the only seller of wheat. That board has everything to say, in consultation with the government, as to

where wheat is to be sold and at what price it is to be sold; and I can guarantee that there will not be any wheat sold into the-United States or anywhere else, other than overseas, while this arrangement exists, at prices which are lower than market prices in those countries, taking into consideration shipping and exchange costs and the duty upon products entering those countries, which has always been done. That position is entirely safeguarded. In other words, we think we are playing the game fairly with the countries with which we are dealing, rather than going back to the "catch as catch can" policies which antagonized our customers in the thirties.
How are we dealing with them? It is true that mutual aid came to an end, but if we want to sell farm products or any other Canadian products to many of these countries at the present time we must be prepared to help finance the sale of such products. At the present time it is not just to say to this house, or to try to leave the impression with the 250,000 farmers of this country, that we are doing something which is not fair to them. We are utilizing all the .economic strength of this country, putting it on the lowest plane possible, to try in the first place to benefit all the people in Canada to the greatest extent possible. Keeping that in mind at all times, we are also endeavouring to assist those people who will be wanting our products in future to consume those products at the present time. That does not apply to anything with greater importance than wheat, bacon, beef and all the other products about which we have talked so much in the last few days.
I now come to a question which has been in the minds of most of those who have been speaking, and for a moment or two I shall deal with the legislation of which there has been some criticism; that is, the bill brought in last session to place floor prices under farm products. I wish to emphasize what I said this afternoon in reply to a question, or an interruption of another speech, that this act is not yet operative. The act was passed last session, and everyone who was in the house at that time understood the terms upon which it was passed. This measure was designed to place what we were pleased to call floor prices under farm products. One can read sections of it and give other interpretations to them, perhaps, but if hon. members will read Hansard to see what was said when this bill was introduced in the house they will find that it says this. We proposed to establish a temporary board. We would appoint the permanent chairman and would take two officials out of the Department of

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
Agriculture and set them up at once to do a job. We may be asked, what was that job. We said the job was to determine the relationship between farm prices as they have been since we established ceilings upon prices in Canada, and the prices of other products farmers had to buy; to study that relationship and get it into the form of figures which might be called parity prices or anything you like. In any event they were to establish the relationship which existed between the ceiling prices as fixed during that period, from 1941 down to the end of the war, and have those facts available for the permanent board which was to be appointed when the War Measures Act went out of existence, to take over the administration of this act. Then we said to the board, in section 9 (1) (a), that they were:
to prescribe from time to time, with the approval of the governor in council, prices at which the board may purchase agricultural products in the market.
Then in paragraph (c) they were directed: to pay to the producers of an agricultural product directly or through such agent as the board may determine the difference between a price prescribed by the board with the approval of the governor in council for such product and the average price, as determined by the board, at which such product is sold in the market during the specified period if such average price is below such prescribed price.
Then in subsection 2, which has been read to the house already by one or two hon. members, there is this provision:
In prescribing prices under paragraphs (a) and (c) of subsection 1 of this section, the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.
If I had time I could read again what was read last night by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), who stated that the president of the farm federation, in speaking of this legislation at the last annual meeting, had declared that for the first time this act gave Canadian farmers an opportunity to enjoy stable prices, and went on to term the prices provided for under this act as parity prices. And I agree with them. Our hon. friends of the C.C.F. party want prices established for the next period of years. Someone has asked how long that period is to be. If they read Hansard they will find that last year someone suggested it should be four years. We refused to make the period four years, on the ground that it might be ten years. It is whatever period is necessary in order to reestablish agriculture in this country on a sound financial basis at the end of
this war. Therefore I say to hon. members to-night that if they want to vote for 100 per cent parity prices all they need do is vote for the policies of the government. Anyone sitting on the other side of the house who, in moving a resolution for floor prices based upon parity, is trying to make the people of this country believe they are moving for something which is not already provided for in the policies of this government, is trying to mislead the voters of this country.
May I say to hon. gentlemen opposite that I agree entirely with the statement made this afternoon by the hon. member for MacLeod (Mr. Hansell), that to indulge in that sort of thing with all the facts before the house is purely and simply playing politics; and I say that knowing that my hon. friends on the other side-
You should know.

I should know, as my
hon. friend says, and I think I do know. And since I do know I want to repeat that that is playing politics, and playing it with a vengeance, by trying to mislead the people.

What I wish to say is
this, that every man who votes against this amendment to-night is voting for parity prices as set up under legislation which the government has already placed upon the statute books. Anyone who votes for the motion tonight is voting for an arrangement of longterm agreements between the countries that use our wheat overseas, particularly Great Britain, and the people and government of Canada-long-term agreements which will establish a stabilized price for our wheat, just as agreements we have had in the last five years have established fair prices and stabilized prices for other farm products of Canada.
Every man who sells hogs knows there never has been a more stabilized price structure for hogs in this country than there has been during the last three years, and particularly the last two. Everyone in Canada knows that, despite what our friends across the way may say, Canada Packers and other packing plants have men out in the province of Ontario at the present time offering over twelve cents a pound for well prepared and well finished beef cattle. That is a higher price than could have been obtained under any policy other than that of the government during recent years. That policy has been one of stabilization.

It is seventeen cents in the
United States.
The Address-Mr. Gardiner

My hon. friend says it
is seventeen cents in the United States. Well, if he went down there to get a shave it would cost him a dollar-and other things in proportion. If he went down there to get a drink it would cost him far more than he pays for it in this country.
We in the Dominion of Canada have controlled prices both on things we produce and on things we consume, and on a very much lower level than they have in the United States. But as long as the level applies right across the board on consumed products as well as on produced, products, nobody will be hurt.
In other words, we have stopped our prices from spiralling, and right now we are stopping them from deflating. The leader of the opposition does not need to worry, so long as this government is in power; and apparently the people of Canada did not worry so long as it was in power. They do not need to worry about deflation-or about inflation, either. We have taken care of inflation during the latter part of the war. We will take care of inflation in the years immediately following the war. And when the time comes when deflation begins to bother us, we have the legislation on the statute books to carry us through. We have agreements made with respect to our farm products to safeguard our farm policy against any of the evils of deflation.

subtopic: ELECTION OF MR. WILLIAM ROSS MACDONALD, MEMBER FOR BRANTFORD CITY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ELECTION OF MR. WILLIAM ROSS MACDONALD, MEMBER FOR BRANTFORD CITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is one matter of procedure which should be dealt with immediately. The rules of the house provide that as soon as possible after the address has been agreed to a deputy speaker of the house should be appointed, also the committees of supply and way and means established. Through the courtesy of hon. gentlemen opposite the committees of supply and ways and means have already been set up. That was done in order to oblige the government in getting through interim supply.
It will not take me more than a minute or two to read to the house the rule which governs in the matter of the appointment of the Deputy Speaker and to propose an hon. member for that position. Standing order 56 respecting the Deputy Speaker reads as follows:
(1)	A chairman of committees of the house, who shall also be Deputy Speaker of the house, shall be elected at the commencement of every parliament, as soon as an address has been agreed on in answer to His Excellency's speech; and the member so elected shall, if in his place in the house, take the chair of all committees of the whole, including the committees of supply and ways and means, in accordance with the

rules and usages which regulate the duties of a similar officer, generally designated the chairman of the committees of ways and means, in the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
(2)	The member elected to serve as Deputy Speaker and chairman of committees shall be required to possess the full and practical knowledge of the language which is not that of the Speaker for the time being.
Mr. Speaker, I would draw attention to the fact that the hon. member to be appointed

to the position of Deputy Speaker must be possessed of the language which is not that of Your Honour, he will therefore be chosen from among the English speaking members of the house. It is desirable that whoever holds the position of Deputy Speaker should possess qualities of mind and temperament similar to your own. He should be courteous, impartial, judicial, possessed of a sense of humour, conciliatory in manner and able to command the confidence and respect of the house in the position which he holds.
The hon. member whose name I should like to put forward is Mr. Ross Macdonald, K.C., of Brantford, Ontario. Mr. Ross Macdonald has been a member of this House of Commons for the last ten years. He was elected to parliament in 1935, 1940 and 1945. He was also a candidate at two previous elections. Mr. Macdonald is a war veteran of the first great war, a graduate of the university of Toronto and of Osgoode Hall, a distinguished member of the legal profession, and may I say, what is important to hon. members of this house, he is wholly familiar with its rules and its procedure and on many occasions in the last parliament, when asked to do so by the Speaker of the house, occupied the chair of the Deputy Speaker, and on occasions the chair of the Speaker of this house. Possessing all the qualities and virtues he does, I hope the house will join unanimously in electing Mr. Macdonald as Deputy Speaker of the house.
I move:
That William Ross Macdonald. Esquire, member for the electoral district of Brantford City, be appointed chairman of the committees of the whole house.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ELECTION OF MR. WILLIAM ROSS MACDONALD, MEMBER FOR BRANTFORD CITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there may not be many occasions in this house when I can support and agree with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the moves he makes. I am glad to say that this is an occasion when I can. It is not my privilege to be personally acquainted with the hon. gentleman who has been nominated to be Deputy Speaker; but on this subject I accept the words of the Prime Minister.
May I say for the members of this party that we extend our sincerest congratulations to the hon. member who has been chosen for that position and that we are sure that he will fill it with distinction to himself and credit to his party. I want to assure him that he will have the utmost cooperation from those of us who sit on this side of the house.

International Labour Conference____

subtopic: ELECTION OF MR. WILLIAM ROSS MACDONALD, MEMBER FOR BRANTFORD CITY
speechtext:
May I join in those congratulations, particularly because I remember the very happy associations that we had with the hon. gentleman who is named Deputy Speaker when we went to Great Britain in 1941. At that time we appreciated the fact that he was the chairman of the delegation and carried himself with distinction to himself and with honour to Canada. I am quite sure that he will fill the position of Deputy Speaker in the same manner in this house. May I also say that the Prime Minister omitted one qualification which I know that the hon. member has. He has not any ancestors; he is married and he has a family.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): The members of my group have something on me in this respect. I have not had an opportunity of meeting the Prime Minister's nominee. But we are happy to join the Prime Minister in his nomination and to offer our congratulations to the hon. member for Brantford City.
Motion agreed to.
